#6265. Quantum energy harvesting could turn an unpredictable source into a predictable charge

Three physicists show on paper that quantum energy harvesting can take power from a jittery source and leave the jitter behind every time.

Electronic devices generally need a stable supply of electricity, and energy picked up from the surroundings is rarely tidy. Smoothing it out first wastes much of what was collected, especially at low voltages.

Three physicists have shown on paper that a tiny quantum system can harvest energy from a jittery source and end up fully charged every time, with none of the jitter.

Oscar Dahlsten, an associate professor of physics at City University of Hong Kong, led the work. His co-authors were Zihan Wang in the same physics department and Fei Meng of the University of Glasgow.

Dahlsten also holds a post at Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen.

Nothing was built. The result is a set of mathematical proofs with one worked example.

The proofs show that the method works with a much wider range of sources than the original proposal considered.

“We initially set out to show that such a protocol might be impossible. To our surprise, our efforts led us to a quantum solution that could achieve exactly the deterministic energy transfer we were looking for,” Dahlsten said.

A rectifier turns a wobbling current into a steady one, and at low voltages it loses a lot. Part of that loss can’t be engineered away.

A perfect rectifier could turn the random jiggling of warm matter into usable current, and that would break the second law of thermodynamics. That law says you can’t get useful work out of heat alone.

Dahlsten’s group proposed a different quantum route to energy harvesting in a 2025 paper.

Instead of smoothing the source, put a quantum system with two energy levels, a qubit, between the source and the device being charged. A qubit has many paths from its low level to its high one.

Many different source behaviors can push the qubit along different paths and still land it on the high level at the same moment, charged, with the source’s randomness left behind.

In that first version, the source was treated as an ordinary wave. Whatever point in its cycle the wave started at, the qubit ended up charged at the same time.

A simple oscillator, such as a pendulum or a spring, responds differently depending on the wave’s starting point and cannot achieve the same predictable result.

Which sources the trick works for was the open question.

The new paper answers that in two steps. First, suppose you don’t know which of several source states you have, only that each one on its own would charge the qubit.

Then the uncertain mix charges it too, because the physics of the mix is the average of its parts.

The second step is where quantum theory does something classical physics can’t.

In quantum theory, one and the same uncertain mix can be described as a blend of entirely different pure states, and no measurement can tell the descriptions apart.

So every pure state in any of those alternative descriptions must charge the qubit as well, and so must any superposition of the original states.

As a result, the family of usable sources widens considerably. The team also calculated how many parameters describe these usable source states.

A plain mix of a given set of states has about as many adjustable knobs as there are states. Their superpositions and mixtures together have roughly that number squared.

A real source is unlikely to match a textbook state exactly, so the team also asked what a slightly wrong source does to the qubit.

They proved that two qubits charged by two slightly different sources can end up no more different than the sources were to begin with.

In classical physics, that guarantee offers little useful information.

That is why classical systems can be so sensitive to their starting conditions.

Two quantum states can be nearly indistinguishable, so a small difference between sources guarantees a small difference in the qubits’ final charge.

The worked example is the simplest quantum model of light meeting matter, a single atom-like qubit and a single mode of the electromagnetic field.

The field states that behave most like a classical wave are called coherent states.

Every coherent state of a given strength, whatever its phase, charges the qubit at the same moment.

So do mixtures of them, and so do superpositions of a wave with the same wave shifted by half a cycle. Physicists call those cat states, and making them has become a central theme of experimental physics.

What can’t work shows up in the same example. A field in thermal equilibrium, warm light at some temperature, always carries some chance of being empty, and an empty field can’t lift the qubit at all.

So heat on its own fails, which fits the second law.

Every result in the paper is a calculation, and the paper names superconducting circuits and single atoms in cavities as the platforms where someone could try it.

Nowhere does the paper estimate how much energy such quantum harvesting could deliver or how quickly.

So there is no figure yet to set against the rectifiers in real devices that gather stray energy from their surroundings.

The authors wrote that the next steps are to extend the argument to systems with more than two levels, and to systems described by continuous variables. New transfer regimes may turn up there.

The full study was published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6263. What can your face reveal about your health? AI finds new clues

AI tools can estimate age and assess cancer survival risk from facial photographs, revealing health clues that may go beyond a patient’s age.

A patient’s appearance can offer doctors clues about frailty and overall health. But those impressions are difficult to measure consistently.

Researchers have developed two artificial intelligence tools that turn facial photographs into estimates of age and survival risk.

The survival tool sorted cancer patients by their risk of death.

In the first test group, patients it put in the highest-risk quarter were more than three times as likely to die as those in the lowest quarter. That gap survived adjustment for the usual clinical factors.

Both programs grew out of one base model built at Mass General Brigham in Boston.

Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist, is the study’s corresponding author. Hugo Aerts, who directs the system’s Artificial Intelligence in Medicine program, is a co-senior author.

“As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy,” Mak said.

“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalized treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”

The base model, called FAHR-Face, was trained on more than 40 million face photographs from a public collection, with no labels attached.

It learned by having patches of each photo hidden and then reconstructing them, which forces a program to pick up how the parts of a face relate to each other.

The team then tuned that base for two jobs.

FAHR-FaceAge learned to estimate age from facial appearance, allowing researchers to explore whether looking older or younger than one’s chronological age relates to health.

It trained on ten public photo collections balanced so that no age group dominated.

FAHR-FaceSurvival learned from 34,363 photographs of cancer patients treated at the Harvard-affiliated hospitals, paired with whether and when each patient died.

“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” Aerts said.

On a public set of photos of presumed healthy people, the age program missed the true age by 5.1 years on average.

A comparable program trained from scratch on the same photos missed by 6.9. The group’s earlier FaceAge model had been built mainly for patients 60 and older; this one spans the whole lifespan.

The team then asked what it means when the program’s estimate runs ahead of a person’s real age.

Among 38,183 cancer patients treated with radiation at the Harvard hospitals, a third looked at least five years older than their age, and 17% looked at least ten years older.

Patients who appeared five or more years older than their age had a 21% higher risk of death over the follow-up period than those who didn’t.

That held after adjusting for age, sex, race, cancer type, and treatment. Patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.

The gap was starkest in the first three months. Among patients the program judged more than 20 years older than their real age, 21.3% died within 90 days. Among those it judged at least ten years younger, 6.4% did.

The survival program skips age altogether and assigns each photo a score from 0 to 1.

The team tested it on photographs of 3,820 patients whose images had not been used to train it.

The scores rose with the seriousness of the cancer, from a median of 0.13 for benign and earliest-stage cases to 0.45 for cancer that had spread.

At the extremes, the scores separated patients sharply. Of 122 patients scored between 0.9 and 1.0, 64 died within 90 days. Of 975 scored at or below 0.1, 20 did.

The two programs relied on different parts of the face.

The survival tool weighed the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose. The age tool weighed the creases from nose to mouth, the forehead, and the temples.

Their outputs were only weakly correlated, and each kept its link to survival when both were in the same model.

“To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph,” Aerts said.

Lifestyle left marks the age program could read. Heavy drinking and drug use went with looking older, and smoking showed the clearest pattern.

Current smokers looked older than former smokers, who looked older than people who had never smoked.

The estimates held up across the things that vary in a real snapshot.

Pose, lighting, facial expression, and makeup made little difference, and most cosmetic surgeries didn’t shift the estimate. Rhinoplasty did, by a small amount.

Both programs were then checked on 4,892 patients treated at Maastricht University‘s radiotherapy clinic in the Netherlands, and both kept their link to survival.

Combining the two scores predicted survival better than either alone.

The survival analyses focused on patients treated at a few centers in wealthy countries.

Whether the scores mean the same thing in other diseases or other parts of the world is untested.

The age tool stratified risk less sharply in Black and Hispanic patients than in White and Asian patients, and the authors wrote that this residual bias remains a risk.

No patient’s treatment was changed by a score. Whether these photo-based scores help doctors select treatments or improve patient outcomes remains unknown.

The authors called for prospective trials before the tools enter routine care.

Mass General Brigham has filed a provisional patent on the next generation of these algorithms, with Mak, Aerts, and lead author Fridolin Haugg named on it.

The team has also opened a public study in which anyone can upload a photo and receive a research readout of their face age.

Those images will be used to test the models on a wider range of people.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Digital Health.

#6262. Nov. 13, 1971: Mariner 9 orbits Mars

On May 30, 1971, Mariner 9 launched, setting off on its mission to Mars. On Nov. 13, 167 days later, it entered orbit around Mars, making it the first spacecraft to orbit another planet.

With Mariner 8, Mariner 9 was one half of the Mars 71 mission. But when Mariner 8 launched on May 9, it failed to achieve orbit and tumbled out of the sky after five minutes, crashing into the Atlantic Ocean. As a result, Mariner 9 inherited all of 8’s goals in addition to its own, giving it an extensive list of objectives: surface mapping, atmospheric monitoring and analysis, surface data collection, and returning around 3,000 photographs.

When Mariner 9 arrived at Mars, it encountered a global dust storm. Because it had been designed for longevity, the orbiter was able to wait out the storm and begin its mission afterwards. (Soviet spacecraft Mars 2 and Mars 3 did not fare as well.) Over the course of about a year, Mariner 9 returned 7,329 photos and mapped 85% of the martian surface. It also revealed a dynamic and active world – including shield volcanoes, dry river valleys, ice at the martian poles – and gave researchers close-up views of the surfaces of Phobos and Deimos.

#6261. The 7 Best Electric Stoves to Upgrade Your Kitchen

These expert-picked models cook cleaner than gas, and offer features like convection and air fry.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Electric stoves burn cleaner and more efficiently than gas—in fact, per the Department of Energy, they’re about three times more energy-efficient than their gas counterparts. They’re also more straightforward to install—no gas line needed—and often feature flat, easy-to-clean, glass-ceramic cooktops. Plus, their ovens preheat quickly and provide even and consistent heat, which is ideal for anyone who loves to bake. The stove delivers the power you want and offers decent oven capacity with 5 cubic feet of space. Dual bake elements in the oven provide more-even cooking. There’s also a full-width storage drawer at the bottom. If you just need your electric stove to handle the essentials at a low price point, look no further. It's also available in a white finish.

This LG range is a smart, energy-efficient pick that pairs a two-speed fan with a powerful rear heating element to preheat faster and bake more evenly across multiple racks. A built-in air fry feature can crisp up wings, fries, and veggies with no preheating, and the roomy 6.3-cubic-foot oven can easily accommodate large dishes, including a 20-pound turkey and the sides.

The five-burner cooktop has a 3,200-watt element that take dishes from a rapid boil to a simmer, with flexible 2-in-1 elements to fit everything from a small saucepan to your largest sauté pan. The slide-in model includes no-preheat air-fry mode and built-in Wi-Fi that lets you control oven functions remotely via the SmartHQ app, compatible with Alexa, Google Assistant, iOS, and Android.

The five-burner cooktop offers versatile heating, and includes a 12-inch/9-inch/6-inch power boil element for rapid heating, plus synchronized burners for large cookware and griddles. Inside, European convection ensures even baking and roasting. The fingerprint-resistant stainless-steel finish keeps it looking pristine outside; a 30-minute steam-clean cycle handles messes inside.

All of these bells and whistles make it a pricier option. And, its glide touch controls, which contribute to the stove’s ultra-modern aesthetic, means that every function is operated via touch—much like swiping on an iPad. If you prefer to use physical knobs, this will not be the best fit.

Built for speed and convenience, this freestanding double oven is a great choice for busy kitchens and home chefs who need flexibility, extra cooking space, and power.

Its five burners include a triple-radiant element that adapts to different cookware sizes while the extra-large European convection double oven—at 6.3 cubic feet, one of the largest in this size—ensures faster, even cooking.

A no-preheat setting lets you cook frozen favorites like pizza and lasagna straight from the freezer, saving time on weeknight meals, and a 50-minute steam-cleaning cycle tackles grime. The only downsides? No Wi-Fi or app support, and surprisingly, no air fry.

While most electric stoves on the market span 30 inches, this sleek freestanding GE model maxes out at just 24 inches across—making it a perfect fit for smaller kitchens. Despite its compact size, it doesn’t skimp on functionality: The front controls are easy to reach, the smooth ceramic glass cooktop wipes clean in seconds, and, thanks to its modular backguard, you can choose to install it with a traditional backguard or flip it down to create a slide-in look.

While there are only four burners, no timer, and a smallish standard (not convection) oven, it’s a stylish, efficient choice for studio apartments, small homes, or anyone cooking for one. It also has a 30-minute steam-clean cycle and a built-in storage drawer that’s deeper than many other stoves on the market. (And if your kitchen can handle a standard-sized stove, GE’s 30-inch free-standing range is a solid, very affordable, choice.)

If you need a stove that’s even more compact than the 24-inch GE, the freestanding 19.5-inch Avanti stove offers serious space efficiency and decent functionality at a very low price. Available in stainless or white, it easily tucks into small kitchens, RVs, and tiny homes. Plus, its retro aesthetic adds a vintage touch.

The four old-school coil burners—three 6-inch and one 8-inch—feature chrome reflector bowls and temperature safety sensors for efficient cooking. While they lack the modern sleekness of a glass cooktop, users report they heat up fast. Inside, the 2.1 cubic feet of oven capacity is roomy enough for one-pan baking and roasting and comes with a broiling pan.

That said, this stove is as basic as it gets. It’s perfect for simple fry-ups and one-pan roasts, but serious home cooks will definitely want more precision and features. If size is your limiting factor, Avanti also makes a more-expensive 19.5-inch glass-top electric stove, which some users say is worth the extra cost, as it provides more even contact with cookware for better heat distribution.

Size can be a significant limiting factor, so measure your stove space first. The standard width for ranges is 30 inches, but if you’re outfitting an apartment kitchen, tiny home, or RV, you’ll want to focus on the few narrower models available.

Next, choose your style: Freestanding stoves have finished sides and back guards, allowing them to stand alone. Slide-in models are designed to sit between cabinets for a seamless look; their stovetops typically sit flush to the back wall, which may require a backsplash update. Drop-in ranges need a custom cabinet base for installation.

Most electric cooktops feature smooth surfaces with heating elements housed beneath tempered glass or ceramic, though traditional coil-style options still exist and tend to be much cheaper. Smooth-top stoves are easier to clean, while coil burners are simpler to replace if one fails.

Standard electric ranges typically come with five burners (four on narrower models). One is often a warming burner, useful for timing multiple dishes. Some models also offer bridge elements—also referred to as "synchronized burners"—which link two burners, handy for griddles or oversized pots. If you frequently boil water, look for one with an express boil burner, designed to heat up faster.

Conventional ovens rely on stationary heating elements—one at the bottom for baking, one at the top for broiling—leading to natural heat rise and possible temperature variations. Standard convection improves on this by adding a fan to circulate hot air for more even cooking. European convection (also called “true” convection) goes a step further, with a third heating element behind the fan for uniform heat distribution across multiple racks.

For everyday cooking, conventional or standard convection works fine. But if you want more precise, even baking and roasting, true convection is worth considering. Be prepared for a slight learning curve if switching to convection, as most recipes are designed for conventional ovens. A good rule of thumb: reduce the temperature by 25°F (e.g., 450°F to 425°F, or 375°F to 350°F), or keep the same temperature but cut the cooking time by about 25 percent. Either way, start checking for doneness earlier than the recipe suggests. A meat thermometer can also help ensure accuracy.

Control panel placement affects both aesthetics and functionality. Backguard controls, found on most freestanding stoves, keep buttons and knobs safely out of reach of children but may be less visually streamlined. Front-control stoves, common in slide-in models, offer a sleek, built-in look and easier access to settings but can be a hazard if you have small kids or frequently lean against the stove while cooking. Many models now include touchscreen controls, which allow for precise adjustments and smart features but may require more care to keep clean.

Many newer electric stoves come with high-tech features designed to make cooking more efficient and hands-free. Wi-Fi-enabled models let you monitor and control your oven remotely via an app—preheating, adjusting temperatures, and setting timers from anywhere. Some even integrate with voice assistants like Alexa or Google Assistant for hands-free commands.

Touchscreen controls and digital displays offer a sleek, modern look, but keep in mind that they can be more finicky than traditional knobs, especially when wet or smudged. If you prefer a more tactile experience, look for models with physical dials or a hybrid control panel.

Some ovens now include built-in air fry functions, which circulate superheated air for crispy, fried-like results without the oil. It’s a great feature for quickly roasting veggies, crisping up frozen snacks, or making healthier versions of fried favorites—no extra countertop appliance needed.

Beyond the sticker price, you’ll want to factor in some extra costs. For one, power cords aren’t usually included in the price, and you can’t reuse your old one. Lowe’s, for example, charges $39.98 to install—which includes a new power cord. Some retailers also charge a separate delivery fee. And, if you’re replacing an existing stove, you should expect to pay around $50 to have your old one hauled away and disposed of. Finally, while most stoves come with a one-year limited warranty (which typically covers manufacturing defects and basic repairs), some retailers offer extended protection plans (for an additional fee) at checkout.

When the glass top of my ancient JennAir electric stove cracked—thanks to a DIY mishap (we stood on it to paint a high part of the kitchen; lesson learned)—I had to find an unplanned replacement. Fortunately, the stovetop still worked, giving me time to explore my options. I visited my local Lowe’s and other reputable retailers to assess everything in person and quickly noticed a difference in selection. Suburban stores only carried standard 30-inch ranges, while city retailers stocked a wider variety, including smaller 24-inch models—something to keep in mind if you’re shopping for a compact space.

I assessed everything: control placement (knobs vs. touchscreen and ease of use), oven heating methods, aesthetics, and extra features like voice control (we’re a household that regularly asks Alexa for help in the kitchen). The models I selected come from trusted brands like GE, Samsung, and Frigidaire, with thousands of positive reviews attesting to their reliability and efficiency. Many are top-sellers across multiple retailers, and some incorporate the latest technology to make cooking faster and more enjoyable. I also chose options across various sizes and price points to fit different spaces and budgets—and included a few solid upgrade picks from the same brands for a slight price increase.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. She’s reviewed everything from roller bags and cameras to hiking equipment and home decor for outlets such as The Montreal Gazette, Fodor's, AFAR, and US Park Pass. Arabella can often be found immersed in DIY projects at her mid-century modern house in upstate New York—a hands-on pursuit that inspires many trips to Lowe’s.

#6260. Wildfire smoke over Borneo hints at danger beneath the forest

A satellite view of Borneo’s wildfires reveals how prolonged drought can put forests and carbon-rich peatlands at risk.

Today’s Image of the Day captures smoke rising from multiple wildfires across Indonesian Borneo, revealing a landscape caught in a severe fire season.

Seen from space, the plumes show how smoke can spread far beyond the fires themselves.

The Copernicus Sentinel-3 mission recorded the scene on October 14, 2026.

Released by the European Space Agency, the image shows the consequences of prolonged dry conditions that have allowed fires to spread.

ESA links the severity of this year’s fires to El Niño, the climate pattern that can reduce rainfall across Indonesia.

The smoke is the most visible part of the story.

Beneath it, damaged forests and vulnerable soils connect the immediate emergency to a longer struggle over how much carbon these ecosystems can keep out of the atmosphere.

A change in the tropical Pacific can alter the weather thousands of miles away.

During El Niño, unusually warm water in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific develops alongside changes in winds and rainfall.

The trade winds that normally push warm surface water westward weaken, and tropical rainfall shifts eastward.

For Indonesia, that shift can mean fewer clouds, less rain, and drought.

A region associated with tropical downpours can enter an extended period in which vegetation and soil steadily lose moisture.

Drought does not supply the spark for every fire. It changes what happens after a fire starts.

Land-clearing practices, forest degradation, and peatland drainage also influence Indonesia’s fire risk.

When those pressures coincide with unusually dry weather, fires have more opportunities to escape and spread.

A recent assessment of the 2026 season identified both El Niño and human-caused warming as contributors to dangerous fire weather.

In parts of Borneo, the fuel extends beneath the forest floor.

Peat forms where waterlogged conditions slow the breakdown of dead vegetation.

Over time, that plant material accumulates, creating a soil rich in carbon. Keeping it wet helps preserve that store.

Drainage changes the balance. As water levels fall, peat becomes more exposed to air and more vulnerable to burning.

Drought can deepen the problem, allowing fires to move from surface vegetation into the ground.

Once established, these underground fires can smolder persistently and prove difficult to extinguish.

NASA’s reporting on Indonesia’s 2026 season described fires burning both at the surface and below it, with dry conditions allowing flames to reach peat deposits that would normally be too wet to burn.

That background helps explain why a smoky satellite scene can represent more than the loss of standing trees.

In peatland areas, a fire may also consume part of the carbon store beneath them.

Forests absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, holding carbon in trunks, branches, roots, and other plant material.

Fire releases some of that carbon back into the atmosphere while damaging the vegetation that would otherwise continue absorbing it.

Peat adds another layer to the loss. Its carbon can remain underground for centuries or longer before drainage and burning release it.

Research in Central Kalimantan, a province in Indonesian Borneo, has documented the release of centuries- to millennium-old carbon following peatland drainage.

Subsequent fires caused further losses, showing how disturbance can dismantle a store that took far longer to build.

The consequences therefore continue beyond the disappearance of the smoke.

Protecting these landscapes means preserving both living forests and the conditions that keep their underlying carbon secure.

A satellite image brings scattered fires into one view, helping reveal an event’s wider reach.

Sentinel-3 also gathers measurements that support more detailed monitoring. Its Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer includes channels designed to detect fires.

Those observations help scientists assess burned vegetation, estimate associated carbon emissions, and examine recovery.

Another instrument tracks vegetation conditions through measurements related to leaves and chlorophyll.

Combined with weather forecasts, satellite observations can help assess forest fire risk and guide prevention efforts.

Today’s image captures Borneo’s fires on October 14, but their effects will outlast the smoke, leaving damaged forests, altered soils, and less carbon stored underground.

#6259. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

L. Davin et al. Modeling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia. PLOS One. 2026. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360388

#6258. Every drop of water has a history, and satellites are tracking the clues

Eight satellites have tracked heavy water isotopes in the air since 2002, and one open database now lines up every reading on a single grid.

A glass of water gives no hint of the ocean it evaporated from or the clouds it rode in on. The molecules do.

A small share of them carry a heavier form of hydrogen, and that share shifts a little with each round of evaporation and rainfall along the way.

This proportion helps researchers trace where water has been.

Eight satellite instruments have measured this proportion in atmospheric water vapor over different periods since 2002, each recording its results in its own format.

A team led from Rice University has now combined their readings into one open database, called WISO-SAT, that anyone can download.

Mampi Sarkar, a research scientist at Rice, led the work with Sylvia Dee, an associate professor in the university’s Earth science department.

Eleven co-authors in the United States, the Netherlands, Germany and Norway brought experience with the individual satellites, including scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

“Most scientists and satellite missions want to share data,” Sarkar said.

“But it’s not always an easy task. Each satellite was designed to answer slightly different questions, so they have all different types of data even though they fundamentally measure the same thing.”

The heavy hydrogen is deuterium, and water that carries it is one of the water isotopes the satellites track. The measure they report is the ratio of those molecules to ordinary ones.

Four of the instruments read heat glowing up from the atmosphere and return a rough vertical profile of that ratio.

The other four read sunlight bouncing off the surface. They return a single value for the whole column of air, weighted toward the lowest layers.

The missions also started and ended in different years, flew at different times of day and stored their results in their own file layouts.

Combining two of them could mean a year of cleaning before any analysis began. Groups around the world could be repeating that labor without knowing it.

“Satellites access regions that field researchers can’t, and they’re incredibly important for consistent, long-term data collection,” Dee said.

“But for this to become a solid resource capturing the enormity of the water cycle, we needed to be able to treat it like one dataset.”

WISO-SAT organizes each instrument’s readings into monthly grids at two resolutions: 1 degree and 5 degrees of latitude and longitude.

A 1-degree cell is about 69 miles (111 kilometers) on a side at the equator. The files run from 2002 to 2024 and carry uncertainty estimates and observation counts where the original data had them.

The files are posted on the Zenodo archive with the code that built them.

“That means you can more easily compare all the datasets, while accounting for differences between instruments, and know exactly where each measurement was taken on the planet and what it’s telling you, no matter which satellite it came from,” Sarkar said.

The instruments keep their own quirks. A profile from one and a column value from another aren’t the same quantity, and the team left them separate rather than blending them.

“It’s so important to highlight that it’s not just the collection of data that matters; it’s also the effort it takes to make the data truly usable for the broader research community, students and even the public,” Dee said.

The database comes with a warning the team tested itself. Satellites see the lower atmosphere poorly. In dry or polar air, their readings drift toward the starting guess built into the software.

The team checked two instruments against water vapor sampled on nine Atlantic research cruises.

One instrument’s readings averaged about 23 parts per thousand higher than the ship measurements, while the other’s averaged about 18 parts per thousand lower.

Compared with measurements from 25 long-term land stations, the second instrument showed an average difference of 67 parts per thousand, with variation around that average roughly twice as large.

A statistical correction based on ground measurements removed those average offsets and improved agreement with the ground data.

The corrections were based on small samples, the authors noted, and one proved unreliable when they repeated the analysis with individual stations removed.

The surface checks covered only the two instruments with vertical profiles and enough overlap with ground data.

How well the sunlight-based column products match the surface remains untested in the database.

For that comparison, the team points users to ground-based column measurements and aircraft profiles.

Dee listed the questions she expects the archive to take on next, from cloud formation and moisture transport to El Niño, deforestation and soil moisture.

The archive is a first version. Its processing code is public so that other groups can grid their own satellite data the same way, and what gets added next depends on who submits it.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Data.

#6257. REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

The smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.

That’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.

At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.

The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.

The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.

The MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.

Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).

In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.

In its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.

The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.

Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

Spectrum Optics MirroSky SkyPilot SP127 Primary Optical Tube: 5-inch 127mm Maksutov-Cassegrain Focal Length: 1900mm Length: 14.6 inches (370 mm) Focal Ratio: f/15 Guide Scope Optical Tube: 53mm ED refractor with Sony IMX662 CMOS camera Focal Length: 200mm Focal Ratio: f/4 Assembled Weight: 26 lbs. (11.8 kg) Mount Payload: 9 lbs. (4 kg) Connectivity: built-in Wi-Fi, 2.4 and 5 GHz Camera Storage: 64GB onboard storage Tripod: Full-size adjustable steel-leg tripod Eyepiece: 25mm Plössl Price: $999.99 Contact: Spectrum Optics 2175 S Grand Ave Santa Ana, CA 92705 1-888-879-5143 spectrumoi.com

For this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.

Setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.

Control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.

Tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.

The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.

I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.

Planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.

Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.

Throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.

I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.

The SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.

Contributing Editor Phil Harrington received the Walter Scott Houston Award in 2018 for his lifelong work in astronomy.

#6256. A massive heatwave wiped out the snow crabs in the Bering Sea, now a rare hybrid crab species has taken over

A snow-Tanner hybrid crab became 13 times more common after the Bering Sea heatwave, and NOAA traced the surge to the snow crab collapse.

The Bering Sea warmed sharply in 2018 and 2019. Shortly thereafter, the crucial snow crab populations behind one of Alaska’s biggest fisheries vanished in one of the largest species die-offs ever recorded in the ocean.

Seven years later, a different crab is filling part of the gap, a cross between the snow crab and its warmer-water cousin, the Tanner crab. Last year that hybrid was 13 times as common as its long-term average.

Erin Fedewa, a fishery biologist at NOAA Fisheries’ Alaska Fisheries Science Center in Kodiak, Alaska, led the study with eight colleagues at the center.

Using the team’s models, the researchers traced the hybrids’ rise to the snow crab collapse itself, not to the warm water.

In an interview with Earth.com, Fedewa said the size of the jump surprised the team. She explained that hybrid crab have been rare in the Bering Sea historically, and not much is known about the factors that affect their abundance.

She emphasized that she “hadn’t expected hybrids to benefit from a marine heatwave and snow crab collapse”

Snow crabs (Chionoecetes opilio) and Tanner crabs (Chionoecetes bairdi) live on the Bering Sea floor in ranges shaped by winter sea ice.

The two meet along a boundary zone. A hybrid is the offspring of one of each, and surveyors recognize one by features that are intermediate between the two parents.

NOAA’s annual trawl survey has counted them since 1988, and before 2025 hybrids never made up more than 10 percent of the males large enough to catch. In 2025, they made up 41.7 percent, about 13 times the historical share.

Nearly half of the catchable males were suddenly not pure snow crab, and the total count of hybrids was nearly triple the survey’s previous record.

Tanner crabs, which do better in warmer water, also reached a record high in 2025. The snow crab population has rebounded quickly since the heatwave too, though the big males that the fishery targets have been slower to return, Fedewa told Earth.com.

Warmer water could have helped hybrids in two ways. The two parent species could have mixed more and produced more hybrids, or the heat could have helped hybrid crabs survive directly.

The team tested both ideas with statistical models built to separate cause from coincidence. Spring sea ice stood in for heatwave conditions, because the heatwave years were nearly ice-free in March and April, with less than 15 percent cover.

Neither warming idea held up. More overlap between the parent species didn’t explain it, and the ice had no direct effect on hybrid numbers. What did show up was a chain.

Less sea ice meant fewer snow crabs, and fewer snow crabs meant more hybrids. That one pathway accounted for 76 percent of the heatwave’s effect on hybrid numbers. The same chain explained the Tanner crab boom.

The likely reason is that snow crabs normally suppress both rivals – Tanners and hybrids – by competing with them or by eating them. When the snow crabs died, that pressure lifted.

Snow and Tanner crabs can’t be aged, so the team couldn’t say exactly how long the chain takes. They reran the models with plausible delays of up to six years and got the same answer each time.

Under current rules, a legal-sized male hybrid can be landed as a snow crab. But hybrids were always so rare that the federal plan behind crab catch limits does not treat them as their own category.

So there is no mechanism for taking hybrid numbers into account when quotas are set.

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game sets the annual catch limits for Bering Sea snow and Tanner crab. Fedewa told Earth.com it could raise the snow crab limit to reflect the harvestable hybrids.

She said that approach is generally not ideal, because it risks putting more pressure on a snow crab population that is still rebuilding. The other option, she said, is for the fleet to land more hybrids within the existing limit.

“If the snow crab fleet harvested and landed more hybrids during the snow crab fishery, this could have the potential to reduce fishing pressure on large male snow crab that we’ve seen much slower recovery of following the collapse,” she said.

The fishery is worth hundreds of millions of dollars a year, and it closed repeatedly after the collapse.

Fedewa was clear that the fishery questions reach beyond what the study tested. The ecological role of the hybrids remains highly uncertain, she said.

So does what their rise means for snow crabs, and for the harvesters, processors and communities that depend on them.

The bigger question is whether the Bering Sea is changing for good. The marine heatwave was part of a longer warming trend that scientists expect to favor Tanner crabs.

Fedewa said it remains uncertain whether the surge signals a lasting shift, from a seafloor community dominated by snow crabs to one that favors crabs suited to warmer water.

The survey that caught the surge runs every year. The next few counts will show whether hybrids stay common or fade as snow crabs make a comeback.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6254. Forever chemicals are supposed to be unbreakable, but new ‘hunter-killer’ chemistry takes them out

A palladium membrane fed hydrogen from inside breaks the bonds in forever chemicals at room temperature instead of just trapping them.

PFAS “forever chemicals” got their name because almost nothing can break them down. They essentially last forever.

Most water filters only trap toxic forever chemicals without actually destroying them. Once the filter is full, that toxic trash still has to go somewhere.

To fix this, scientists invented a new metal-coated filter that uses hydrogen gas to completely break the chemicals apart.

By swapping out the atoms that make these chemicals so tough, the new filter destroys them at normal room temperature.

In tests, it wiped out over 90 percent of the chemicals, proving we can finally destroy this pollution instead of just moving it from the water to a landfill.

Bruce Rittmann, who directs the Biodesign Swette Center for Environmental Biotechnology at Arizona State University, led the work with Min Long and Jie Cheng.

Colleagues at Rice University, the National University of Singapore and two universities in China also took part. The whole study ran in a glass reactor about a foot (30 centimeters) long.

“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” Rittmann said. PFAS is the family’s chemical name, and the chemicals are in water, soil, food and people.

“We all have PFAS in us,” he said. “They stay in the environment. They move up the food chain, and so they’re a big legacy problem.”

PFAS, or forever chemicals, are chains of carbon atoms wrapped in fluorine. The coating is what lets nonstick pans and waterproof jackets shed oil and water, and it’s in firefighting foam too.

“It’s called the strongest bond in organic chemistry,” Rittmann said.

In 2024, the EPA set drinking water limits of 4 parts per trillion for PFOA (perfluorooctanoic acid) and PFOS (perfluorooctanesulfonic acid). Three others, including GenX, got a limit of 10 parts per trillion.

The reactor holds 120 hollow plastic fibers coated with a film of palladium. Hydrogen gas is pumped into the hollow core of each fiber, so it reaches the palladium from underneath while the contaminated water sits against the outside.

Palladium splits hydrogen molecules into single atoms. Some stay on the metal’s surface, and others slip in between the palladium atoms and are stored inside the metal, which swells by about 4 percent as it fills.

The study’s central finding is that the two kinds of hydrogen do different jobs.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann explained.

In control runs, hydrogen without palladium did nothing to PFOA. Palladium without hydrogen took about 30 percent of the PFOA out of the water but released no fluoride, likely because the molecules stuck to the metal without breaking.

Hydrogen on the surface helps the membrane capture a PFAS molecule and hold it flat against the metal. The hydrogen stored inside the metal supplies the energy that swaps a fluorine atom for a hydrogen atom, one bond at a time.

Chains with no fluorine left were among the end products.

The team tested that by feeding hydrogen either through the fiber cores or into the air space above the water. PFOA left the water at about the same rate either way. However, feeding through the fibers doubled the rate at which fluoride was released.

The team also ran a commercial palladium-on-carbon catalyst, which holds stored hydrogen for a shorter time. It removed about 85 percent of the PFOA but freed only 37 percent of the fluorine, compared with 51 percent for the membrane film.

In an interview with Earth.com, Rittmann said the way the gas arrives is what sets this reactor apart. Delivering hydrogen straight to the base of the palladium film creates a highly reactive palladium hydride, and that, he said, is what speeds the reaction up.

In the batch tests, each chemical spent 44 hours in the reactor on its own, in water acidified to pH 4, which is more acidic than tap water.

The longer the carbon chain, the faster the chemical was removed and the more of its fluorine came off. PFNA (perfluorononanoic acid), with nine carbons, lost 59 percent of its fluorine.

In contrast, four-carbon PFBS (perfluorobutane sulfonate) lost 26 percent, while PFOA, PFOS and PFHxS (perfluorohexanesulfonic acid) fell in between.

A longer chain sticks to palladium more strongly, the team’s calculations found, and it carries more of the weaker carbon-fluorine bonds that hydrogen can attack first.

GenX didn’t follow the pattern. It has six carbons but an oxygen atom linking two halves of its chain, and that link made it stick less and resist more. Only 27 percent of its fluorine came off, about the same as PFBS.

For Rittmann, the point of the paper is that the membrane took apart all six regulated forever chemicals, which argues for one mechanism that should work across the family.

He told Earth.com that “more than 20,000 PFAS compounds have been produced, and many more than the six are in use.”

For the long test, the team mixed all six chemicals into one feed at 50 micrograms per liter each and pumped it through the reactor without a break.

Over 58 days the membrane removed between 93 and 99 percent of every compound, and the fluoride in the outflow works out to 83 percent of the fluorine coming off.

Fifty micrograms per liter is also 50,000 parts per trillion, more than 10,000 times the EPA limit for PFOA. In no run did the water reach the drinking-water limits themselves. About 10 percent of the palladium was lost over the run.

“I was not at all surprised that we had good long-term performance,” Rittmann said.

His group has run these reactors for longer than 58 days, he said, and has measured the palladium loss directly and found the rate very low. The catalyst keeps working as long as it is not overloaded with PFAS.

“Palladium is expensive,” Rittmann said. “It’s around $50,000 a kilogram.”

Using less of it was not part of this study, Rittmann said, but finding a way to do so “is one of our prime topics these days.”

One approach he would describe is a biofilm, a layer of bacteria that builds up on the outside of the fibers and holds the palladium particles in place.

With the metal inside that film, the palladium reaction and the bacteria’s own breakdown of the chemicals run side by side. “This makes the overall process notably faster,” he said.

Arizona State also described a role alongside existing treatment. Carbon filters or a conventional membrane would first concentrate the PFAS from a large volume of water into a small waste stream. The palladium membrane would then destroy that stream instead of storing it.

Every feed in this study was mixed in the lab, and the team reports no test on water from a real contaminated site.

Whether the membrane can take forever chemicals from parts per billion down to the parts-per-trillion limits that utilities must meet is still an open question.

The group is now scaling the reactor up for pilot tests through a spin-off company, Metric Water Catalyst.

“If things go well, we may be able to do pilot testing in 2027,” Rittmann said.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6253. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6252. One day of fatty food was enough to trigger a surprising response in the mouse brain

A high-fat diet changed brain cells involved in eating and weight control within a single day in male mice, revealing an unexpected early response.

Weeks of fatty food are known to blunt a group of brain cells in mice that hold back eating. That reduced activity may contribute to further overeating and weight gain.

Earlier studies measured the cells after at least two weeks on a high-fat diet, leaving their initial response unclear.

Yi Lu and Mark Rossi at Rutgers University examined that initial response and found a different pattern.

After a single day of high-fat food, the cells in male mice fired more easily than before, which the authors read as the brain trying to limit weight gain.

In female mice, the same cells already fired easily on a normal diet, and the fatty food didn’t change that.

The cells are in the lateral hypothalamus, a region near the base of the brain that helps control eating and has been studied as a feeding center since the 1950s.

Rossi is an assistant professor at Robert Wood Johnson Medical School and a resident scientist at the Child Health Institute of New Jersey.

He has spent years on one group of those cells, the ones that release the signaling chemical glutamate. Switching those cells on makes a mouse eat less, so the team calls them a brake.

Lu recorded from single cells in thin slices of mouse brain, using a glass pipette fine enough to seal onto one neuron and read its electrical activity.

Pushing a small current into each cell showed how readily it fired.

On a normal diet, the brake cells in females fired more times for the same push than the cells in males did. Their electrical spikes were also narrower.

Female cells also received inhibitory signals from neighboring cells more often, so they were both easier to fire and more often held back.

The baseline recordings came from 40 cells in three male mice and 51 cells in three female mice.

The team also recorded cells from other mice after one, two, or seven days on a high-fat diet.

Fat supplied 60% of the calories in the experimental diet, compared with 21% in the mice’s usual chow.

In males, one day was enough. The brake cells fired more for the same current, and they needed less current to fire at all. The change was there on day one, day two, and day seven.

In females, the firing rate was unchanged at the one-, two-, and seven-day measurements.

The team wrote that the male result surprised them, since the two-week studies had pointed the other way.

The signals arriving at the cells shifted too, but not in the same direction. In males, the excitatory inputs that drive these cells grew less frequent.

In females, it was the inhibitory inputs that dropped, and only briefly: by day seven they were back to normal.

The input recordings came from just two mice per group, which the authors list as a limit on what they can say about them.

A cell that fires more easily on fatty food could be part of the problem or part of the body’s defense.

To tell which, the team gave the brake cells a bacterial sodium channel called NaChBac, which keeps them in a more excitable state. Then they weighed the mice every day for a week.

Male mice with the extra excitability gained less weight than control males, on normal chow and on the fatty diet alike.

Female mice on chow were unaffected, which the authors think fits with their cells already being excitable. Female mice on the fatty diet lost weight.

The treated mice weren’t eating less. Over six hours with the fatty food in front of them, treated mice of both sexes ate more of it.

Their activity in an open arena didn’t change either.

The authors wrote that the weight difference most likely comes from the mice burning more energy, though they didn’t measure that directly.

Female mice tend to put on weight more slowly than males on a high-fat diet, and the authors see the brake cells as one reason why.

In males, the quick response may hold off some weight gain before the longer-term blunting sets in.

Raising the cells’ excitability, the authors wrote, may limit weight gain without reducing food intake.

Everything here happened in mice, and in a region of the brain where many kinds of cells are mixed together.

The recordings couldn’t separate the subtypes of brake cells, so the team can’t say which ones changed.

Nor can they say whether the shift in incoming signals came from the cells sending them or from the connections themselves.

Why the female cells start out more excitable is also open. Males and females often respond differently to fasting and overfeeding, and removing the ovaries from female mice makes them gain weight the way males on fatty food do.

The authors expect estrogen to be involved, but this study tested no hormone.

The biggest open question is how a brake that fires more easily on day one ends up blunted by week two.

The team suspects the cells recalibrate under sustained pressure, the way neurons across the brain adjust to a lasting change in their input.

No one has yet recorded the same cells across that whole stretch. The authors wrote that a study following them from the first day to the second week is what it would take.

The full study was published in the journal The Journal of Neuroscience.
