#6250. How to watch Starship Flight 15

SpaceX is set to launch its 15th test flight of Starship on Friday, Nov. 13. For the first time, the company will try to catch both stages of the rocket — the Super Heavy booster and the upper stage, which SpaceX calls “Ship” — with the arms of its launch tower. If it works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full.

SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (4:45 p.m. CST) Friday from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, pending regulatory approval. Starship launch dates often slip, so check the company’s Flight 15 mission page for the latest.

SpaceX’s live webcast begins about 30 minutes before liftoff — around 5:15 p.m. EST if the launch holds at the start of the window. You can stream it on the Flight 15 mission page or on SpaceX’s X account.

If you’re near the Texas-Mexico border, crowds typically gather on South Padre Island, across the bay from the launch site. On the Mexican side, the public beach at Playa Bagdad offers a head-on view of the launch tower.

About six and a half minutes after liftoff, Super Heavy should fly back to Starbase and be plucked from the air by the tower’s “chopstick” arms, a catch SpaceX has made three times before. Ship will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites.

The real test comes the next day. Ship will circle Earth about 14 times at roughly 171 miles (275 kilometers) up before heading home. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea: it flips upright, and then fires its engines to set down gently on the water. This time, it will run that same maneuver over Starbase and hopefully settle into the tower’s arms instead. SpaceX’s flight timeline puts the catch about 22 and a half hours after launch — around 4:18 p.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 14, if Starship lifts off on time.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for reentry, the landing burn, and the final approach is healthy. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with go/no-go checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6249. A tube made of tiny speakers is called ‘the closest thing to magic’ this scientist has ever seen

Finnish physicists turned ultrasound into a sound tube with no walls that steers water, powder, gas and even sparks along bendable paths.

Making water flow horizontally through the air without spilling sounds like magic. But scientists in Finland just made it happen by inventing a brand new kind of pipe.

Instead of using plastic or metal, they built an invisible tube out of sound waves that holds a stream of liquid perfectly in mid-air.

Ari Salmi and Dmitry Nikolaev of the University of Helsinki built the device with colleagues at the Public University of Navarre in Spain and the University of Michigan.

A ring of 256 small ultrasonic speakers, each about the size of a shirt button, surrounds the water from about 2 inches (5 centimeters) away. They push on it from every side, but a person standing next to the ring doesn’t hear a thing.

“Of all the experimental setups I have seen, I would say this is the closest thing to magic,” said Salmi, a professor of electronics who led the development of the device.

The same ring, driven differently, guided powder, mist, two heavy gases and even an electric spark along paths the team could bend on command. So far it works over a stretch about 3 inches (8 centimeters) long.

Sound is pressure moving through air. A loud enough sound pushes on whatever it meets. Labs have used that push for decades to float a drop of water or a small bead in mid-air.

Levitation of that kind moves one object, or a few, at a time. Alternatively, it needs a solid vibrating surface underneath. A wall-free channel that carries a flowing stream and bends on command is the new part.

The Helsinki team worked out how to time the 256 speakers so that their waves add up into a long, thin field. Its strongest pressure wraps around a quiet core, like the walls of a hose. Anything inside gets pushed back toward the center whenever it drifts.

Change the timing and the field bends. The team sent the water straight through the sound tube, then tilted it left and right. They shifted where the water landed by about six-tenths of an inch (16 millimeters) without losing a drop.

Salmi, answering questions from Earth.com together with Nikolaev, said the thing that surprised them most was simple. “We were surprised that the ultrasonic pipe does not leak,” he said.

The sound tube has settings, and different forms of matter need different settings. A field shaped like a long donut, with high pressure around a hollow center, held a stream of water in place.

It also held single drops about a sixteenth of an inch (1 to 2 millimeters) across.

The donut field failed on fine powder, though. Grains of silica about the width of a human hair started circling inside it. They were caught in a slow swirl of air that the sound itself stirs up. The swirl flung them out.

A field with petal-shaped lobes around the center kept the powder on track instead. Only a few stray grains fell along the way.

Gases needed a third setting, with the pressure focused down the middle.

Carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide, both heavier than air, followed the field in a hollow sheath around that core. So did the mist from a household humidifier. Helium, which is lighter than air, couldn’t be steered at all in these tests.

“By changing how the speakers are controlled, we can reshape and turn the tube as needed,” said Nikolaev, a postdoctoral researcher who led the team on the project.

“Transporting a solid substance, for example, requires a different field configuration than transporting a liquid or a gas.”

The strangest passenger in the sound tube was a spark. The team put the tip of a small Tesla coil inside it. With the sound off, its discharge jumped in random directions and wandered as much as an inch (25 millimeters) from side to side.

With the sound on, the spark locked onto the path that the field traced. It strayed by only about a millimeter, roughly the width of the glowing channel itself.

A spark heats a thin thread of air, and the authors argue that the same sound pressure that steers a gas steers that thread.

The team used the steered spark to weld the edges of two plastic pieces without touching them.

Other demonstrations in the paper spelled the letter E in water drops on a plate and filled rows of tiny wells with liquid or powder. One merged two liquid streams in mid-air.

The tricks point at 3D printing. Powder came through the ring at about a seventh of an ounce (4.2 grams) a minute, near the low end of what metal printers feed. Liquid came through at up to 1 fluid ounce (30 milliliters) a minute, more than most printers that lay down living cells push.

The ring runs at about 40,000 vibrations a second, too high-pitched for a human ear to register. The pressure inside isn’t gentle.

“At the core of the device, the intensity of the ultrasound is comparable to a continuous roar of gunfire right next to your ear,” Nikolaev said. “But it is too high-pitched for the human ear.”

Salmi said the idea came to him on an evening dog walk four years ago. His lab had built a device that cleaned the insides of pipes with ultrasound. At lunch, a colleague had remarked that it would be handy if a pipe had no surface for dirt to stick to.

The University of Helsinki has filed a patent application on the method, naming Salmi and Nikolaev among the inventors.

The prototype is a tabletop device. In their answers to Earth.com, Salmi and Nikolaev said it’s meant for small, delicate flows rather than anything resembling plumbing.

They expect the stream’s width can grow to about an eighth to a fifth of an inch (3 to 5 millimeters).

The field is also easily disturbed. Any turbulence in a gas stream broke the guidance. The researchers had to drape fabric around the device to block drafts in the room.

Sound bouncing around inside the cylinder weakened the field more than their calculations predicted, which is one reason they built the steering section as a widening cone.

The first real jobs, the two researchers told Earth.com, will likely be moving gases, “since there are very few current methods that can do that.”

They added, “We find the universality of the method very intriguing – it works with all states of matter (solids, liquids, gases and plasma).”

Whether chained modules can carry a stream across a bench, or a room, is the question a 3-inch prototype can’t answer. The team’s code for shaping the fields is public, so other labs with speaker arrays can now try.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6247. Climate change is unfolding very differently just inches above the ground

Microclimate research finds climate change can warm one slope while cooling another nearby, and most wildlife lives in that near-ground air.

Climate change usually arrives as one number for a whole region: so many degrees warmer than it used to be.

A regional average may reveal little about the conditions a beetle, seedling or toad experiences near the ground.

New research finds that air near the ground can warm much faster than the regional average, barely at all, or even cool while the region heats up.

The clearest example in the review is a patch of coast in southwest England about 1.2 miles (2 kilometers) on a side.

A computer reconstruction of its hottest days from 1983 to 2015 put the regional warming at about half a degree Fahrenheit (0.3°C). Inside that patch, one spot warmed by 5.2°F (2.9°C) and another cooled by 2.3°F (1.3°C).

Same coast, same three decades, opposite directions.

Caroline Greiser, a researcher at Stockholm University and its Bolin Centre for Climate Research, led the review with 20 colleagues from Europe, South Africa and the United States.

They call this near-ground climate the microclimate, and it doesn’t change at the same rate as the climate around it.

“Climate change is often described as a single number for a region. But organisms live in specific places – in a particular patch of forest or on a particular slope. The climate they experience can change at a very different rate from the regional average,” Greiser said.

The regional number comes from weather stations, which are deliberately placed in open spots away from trees and slopes.

It also comes from climate models that work on grid squares 6 to 60 miles (10 to 100 kilometers) across. Neither can see the shade under a shrub.

The review doesn’t report new field measurements.

It pulls together published work from atmospheric science and ecology and adds three computer simulations of real landscapes, run with models built by Ilya Maclean of the University of Exeter.

The simulations track the air 2 inches (5 centimeters) above the ground, where many small land animals and seedlings live.

The physics is simple to state. Sunlight that reaches the ground either warms the surface and the air above it, evaporates water, or gets stored in soil and plants.

Anything that shifts that split shifts the temperature a small creature feels.

A 2022 study found that daytime cloud cover over Europe fell by roughly 1.5% to 2% between the periods 1980 to 1995 and 2000 to 2015.

Extra sun on a clear day lands far harder on a south-facing slope than on a forest floor, so an uneven landscape gets more uneven as the clouds thin out.

At night, clouds catch heat rising off the ground and send part of it back down, which can keep near-ground temperatures warmer than on a clear night.

On a clear, calm night, cold air drains downhill and collects in hollows, and a valley bottom can frost while the slope above it doesn’t.

The team’s simulation of a landscape in the Spanish Pyrenees put numbers on this.

Doubling the cloud cover instead of halving it lowered near-ground temperatures on the hottest days of the year by about 22°F (12.4°C) on average, with the strongest cooling on open ground.

The same change in the sky cooled some patches far more than others.

Snow mattered most on the coldest nights. A snow blanket raised minimum near-ground temperatures by about 5.4°F (3°C) on average, roughly ten times the effect of wind or air humidity.

Where winter snow is disappearing, that insulation goes with it.

Warming is pushing shrubs and trees into grasslands and tundra in many parts of the world.

The review’s third simulation took a 0.4-square-mile (1-square-kilometer) patch of the Anatolian steppe in Turkey and filled it in with the shrubs and trees growing at a nearby site.

On the hottest days of the year, near-ground temperatures fell by up to 30°F (16.6°C) under tall, dense shrubs and trees, while open patches where the model made the grass shorter warmed by up to 11°F (6°C).

The same landscape, under the same sky, went two directions at once.

“Vegetation is not simply responding to climate change – it can also modify the climate experienced by organisms living under canopies,” Greiser said.

“When vegetation changes, it changes the local energy balance, and this can lead to very different temperature trends within the same landscape.”

Smaller shifts are already under way. In a mixed forest in New Hampshire, spring leaves came out earlier between 1982 and 2019.

The review’s second simulation found that the extra April leaf cover changed the forest floor’s minimum and maximum temperatures by only about a third of a degree Fahrenheit (0.2°C) each.

The shade can also vanish fast. Droughts, insect outbreaks, fires and storms strip canopies, and a single disturbance can expose a forest floor to conditions equal to several decades of regional warming at once.

Earth.com has reported the same pattern after bark beetle outbreaks and in fragmented forests.

Which plants take over matters too. In a large tree-planting experiment in China, plots with 24 tree species grew denser canopies than single-species plots, and the ground beneath them was up to 7.9°F (4.4°C) cooler.

In the Arctic, shrubs replacing pale lichen can reflect only half as much sunlight, because dark vegetation absorbs far more than lichen or snow.

Jonas Lembrechts of the University of Antwerp is a senior author on the review.

He and his co-authors point to the growing number of long-term near-ground temperature records as the way to check simulations like these against measurements taken on the ground.

Cool pockets, such as forested slopes and basins where cold air pools, might warm more slowly than the open ground beside them. The review finds the evidence for that mixed.

Forty-five years of records from a forested mountain watershed showed little difference in long-term warming between sites, despite frequent cold-air pooling.

Across Austria, by contrast, winter temperature inversions became 11% less frequent between 1961 and 2017, and low-lying sites warmed faster as a result.

The mixed evidence is the practical problem. Predictions of where species can live are mostly built from regional climate data.

The authors argue those predictions will keep misjudging which populations are safe until they account for what happens at ground level.

“If we want to understand where species will persist and where they will be most vulnerable, we need to know not only how the regional climate is changing, but also how that change translates into the microclimates organisms actually experience,” Greiser said.

The simulations changed one thing at a time, clouds or wind or snow, while holding everything else steady.

Real weather changes several of them at once, so the team describes the runs as illustrations of single mechanisms rather than forecasts.

The landscape model also leaves out cold air draining downhill, so real patterns are probably patchier than the maps show.

The review also deals mostly in averages, which the authors wrote can hide the heat waves and frosts that actually push a species out of a place.

The hardest open problem they name is physical.

How heat and moisture move through a tangle of branches and leaves is still hard to quantify, so how strongly vegetation shields or amplifies warming remains uncertain.

Long-term records that track vegetation and near-ground temperature together, in the same places, are what would settle it. Those paired records remain rare.

“The processes that determine microclimate are complex and involve both atmospheric and biological systems. Understanding them therefore requires collaboration between atmospheric scientists and ecologists,” Greiser said.

The full study was published in the journal Global Change Biology.

#6246. The 9 Best Multitools for Fixing Things in a Pinch

Cut, tighten, loosen, open, and twist your way through whatever challenges crop up.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool. These handy pocket-size companions have come a long way from the Swiss Army Knives of yesteryear, boasting major improvements not just in overall design, but in the quality of tools, materials, and the total number of features offered. Modern-day multitools are designed to be twisted, wrenched, and squeezed with just about the same force that any regular item in your toolbox endures.

A good multitool is typically made of all-stainless steel or equally durable metal with as many as 30 tools integrated into the frame. That said, the majority of them still fit comfortably in a pocket and weigh less than a half pound.

There are dozens of multitool manufacturers, so we got our hands on models from established, popular brands like Victorinox, Gerber, Leatherman, SOG, and more to find out which stood out from the pack. Following our tests and in-depth research, these are the multitools we pick up for fixing nearly anything in a pinch.

It’s hard to nail down one aspect of the Arc that I like best, because it does just about everything well. The opening and closing mechanism is responsive and every tool is accessible from the outside. Plus, the 20 listed functions all work well, as opposed to those on some other multitools that feel like afterthoughts for the sake of an eye-popping marketing claim. This effectiveness across the board is precisely why it is our new best overall pick.

In comparison to our former best overall pick, the Victorinox Spirit X, the Arc shines the brightest when looking at its blade. Unlike the Spirit X, which is made entirely of stainless steel, the knife on the Arc is made of MagnaCut. That means it’s more resistant to corrosion and rust and retains its edge longer.

Beyond this, the blade is simply wider, longer, and based on a pretty basic touch test, feels a lot sharper. In my hands, it made it easier to poke through boxes sealed with duct tape and slice off a chunk of an apple.

The Arc also comes with a larger set of scissors, a thicker saw, and a larger file. Furthermore, it’s equipped with a hip clip that slides directly onto your pants while the Spirit X requires a holster that must be looped through your belt to carry it on your person outside of a pocket.

RoverTac’s 12-in-1 initially caught our eye because it has a good number of useful tools—and it’s affordable, too. While it might be bulky and heavy, we have to admit it’s a decent value. We don’t expect it to hold up to intense use, but in a “save your butt” kind of capacity, it’s certainly holds up to light use.

The long-nosed pliers, wire cutter, and wire stripper all worked reasonably well, as did the can and bottle openers and various screwdrivers. RoverTac claims the tool includes a saw blade, but it’s more like a serrated knife, which worked—just not very well.

The plain knife blade is sharper than it looks and easily cut through rope and twine during our tests. The 12-in-1 comes with a sewn nylon sheath to attach to your belt. Don’t expect this to be the pride of your tool collection, but when you need it most, it will be there.

While no multitool can replace a set of full-size hand tools, the Gerber Gear Center-Drive multitool is by far the closest that we’ve tested. The foldable center-axis provides a lot more length in comparison to the average multitool screwdriver, which gives you extra reach for tight spaces.

The blade on the Center-Drive is also the longest of any that we’ve tested. It feels large enough to take on real cutting responsibility like thick rope or small branches. The high-carbon steel also ensures long-term durability so you don’t have to worry about constantly sharpening the blade between uses.

The Center-Drive is bulkier than other options on this list, but the included nylon sheath is designed to slip onto your belt. Another plus is that there’s a full bit set included.

Fresh out of the box, the Swiss Tool Spirit X impressed us with its design and finish. The tools are packed into the frame very closely, like scientific instrumentation. All the tools—save one—deploy from the outside of the frame, so you can access them without much hassle. The company claims 24 tools in this multitool, but we counted 23, including one that’s simply a hook for a lanyard.

While the needle-nose pliers, wire cutters, scissors, three standard screwdrivers, and can opener work well, it was the less common tools that really impressed us. This is the first multi we’ve seen with a metal saw, which is on the edge of the file. It cut through mild steel hardware surprisingly well, and the file did a nice job cleaning up the edges when we were done.

The Phillips screwdriver shank flares out at the end so that all four points on the head are the same size, making for very solid engagement. The Spirit X’s bottle opener is made from wide stainless steel stock, which keeps it flat on the bottle cap so it doesn’t slip or cut into the cap. The combination reamer-punch efficiently opens up holes in wood, leather, and soft metals, and it can drill holes through 3⁄4-inch pine board.

An all-around great pick, this multitool will get the job done, no matter what that job happens to be.

Full Victorinox Swiss Tool Spirit X Multitool Review

The next iteration in one of Leatherman’s most popular lines comes with a weighty price tag. But it’s justified, since we had a hard time finding fault with the Wave Alpha.

The multitool comes with a standard knife blade, a saw, a file, and a pair of scissors. The file worked well smoothing out nails, and the saw comfortably powered through small branches.

However, we were most pleasantly impressed with the scissors. They’re much larger than any other pair of scissors we've seen on a multitool (“the largest cutting surface ever on a pliers-based Leatherman,” according to the brand). Because of their size and the spring that pushes the handle back up after every snip, we were able to hold the bottom still in hand and easily use our thumb to press down on the blade to cut. This simplified cutting through large pieces of paper, even for those of us who are lefties (since nearly no scissors are designed for cutting with our dominant hand).

The classic pocket knife is made of MagnaCut steel, which is corrosion-resistant and has great edge retention. During testing, we focused on everyday items like twine, paper, cardboard, and zip ties and opening sealed packages. We never needed more than one stern pull of the blade to get through any of them.

The central tool of the Wave Alpha is the plier-wire cutter, which we found easy to use thanks to the biting grip of the ridges and the ergonomic handle.

Though Leatherman lists 16 tools, we counted closer to 12. For instance, the file is designated as two separate tools, with the traditional flat side counting as one and the diamond-coated edge counting as another. That’s a fairly common embellishment with multitool descriptions.

Full Leatherman Wave Alpha Multitool Review

With its svelte, minimalist frame featuring three main tools, this Gerber cuts down on the unnecessary junk and keeps its tools simple and effective.

As a pocket knife–based multitool, it features a full 3-inch, locking plain blade. Although it isn’t the sharpest right out of the box, it cut cleanly through paper, plastic, rope, twine, and steak, and was adequate for some light whittling.

The side opposite the blade features a hex bit driver and scissors. The driver has a reversible bit in a magnetic holder—we love this because you get legit flat and Phillips screwdrivers that just plain work.

The scissors are a bit larger than those found on other models and were easy to control when cutting out intricate shapes from paper to medium cardboard. Between the scissors and the driver is a sharp, narrow awl. We weren't able to use this to drill holes in wood and plastic, but it works well, as intended, to poke holes through leather and canvas.

Rounding out the eight functions is a nice bottle opener that pivots off the end of the tool frame. It doubles as a pry bar (the bottle opener flipped over) and a “hammer” (the wide base of the bottle opener). Is it less a hammer and more just a flat surface for hitting things? Sure. But when you need to finish tapping in a tent stake or small nail, it’ll do.

The plier-based Leatherman Signal comes with several standard items, including a stainless steel blade and a serrated saw. However, it impressed us most with its several outdoor-specific functions.

These include a detachable ferro rod that, in combination with the serrated saw, creates sparks for your campfire. The ferro rod also doubles as an emergency whistle. During testing, I was particularly pleased with the carabiner on the bottom of the multitool. While not a major feature, being able to clip it onto my hiking backpack and forget about it made it so much easier to carry with me than other options.

Perhaps the only major downside is the hammer tool. It functions more like a blunt, flat end you can use in a pinch.

Everyday life doesn’t always require a saw, hammer, or bulky pliers. The Leatherman Micra is a keychain tool, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything else. The Micra hosts a number of items that are still quite handy when small and, importantly, are often the most useful in day-to-day life.

The multitool is built around a pair of scissors, which are the perfect size for cutting tags and snipping loose threads. Tools on the body include tweezers, a nail file and cleaner, a small screwdriver, and a bottle opener, among others.

While carrying the Leatherman Micra around, I was genuinely astonished at how often I used it. I frequently pulled it out for small tasks like picking something out from under my nails, plucking a small hair out of place, or tightening the screws on my sunglasses’ hinges.

The Micra works so well because it knows what it is. The convenience and portability make it hard to go anywhere without it.

With its wide frame and large plier jaws, the Dual-Force is a beast of a multitool. You can open the pliers and slip the pivot to spread the dual-position jaws extra wide to grab large fasteners or objects. The jaws feature three separate gripping areas: two for large or small round objects and one for gripping flat things. We appreciated their versatility for holding well in a variety of situations.

One of our favorite things about the Dual-Force is that all the other tools are accessible when the pliers are closed. This multitool also features a bit holder with two Phillips and one plain screwdriver bit. We regard these among the most useful multitool screwdrivers available, although they are sometimes difficult to use in tight spaces.

The Dual-Force is rounded out with a large knife, a saw blade, and a three-sided file. The knife blade is reasonably sharp out of the box, and we easily cut through thick rope with it. We used the saw blade to cut both green and dried-out sticks and branches with relative ease. We were able to use the file on both wood and metal, although it was better suited for the metal.

While the number of tools and functionalities on your multitool isn’t the only measure of how helpful it’ll be, it does give you a sense of its versatility. The multitools we recommend have anywhere from five to 20 or more different functions.

Note that, in their descriptions, manufacturers often count different capabilities of a specific tool individually to arrive at a higher number of “tools.” Pliers, for example, may be counted three or four times if they can function as needle-nose pliers, regular pliers, wire cutters, and wire strippers.

It’s key to pay attention to the quality of each tool and, of course, how often you’ll use them. For instance, a multitool with a screwdriver attachment is great, but if that multitool’s grip doesn’t give you the leverage to twist off seized screws or only comes with one screwdriver bit, it’s far less effective in practice.

We recommend starting your search by listing three or four tools you use most. Then, opt for a multitool that performs well at those functions. A multitool that has a few tools you use frequently will end up being more valuable to you than one packed to the brim with tools you don’t use much at all.

One of the key reasons to own a multitool is for its portability and convenience compared with carrying a full set of tools. So, if you can’t fit it in a pocket or in the center console of your car, it’s probably too big. That said, size isn’t everything. Each item on a multitool needs enough space from the others to work effectively, and you need to make sure you have a good grip for leverage.

The weight of a multitool only becomes a problem if it is too heavy to comfortably clip onto a belt or slip into a pocket. The majority of the tools on our list are made of stainless steel, which is durable yet relatively lightweight.

Can a Multitool Replace a Tool Kit? In short, no. Multitools are useful in a pinch or when you just need them for a quick fix, but they cannot replace a full tool kit. The biggest utility of a multitool is its convenience. It can function well enough for small repairs or to get by when you’ve got nothing else nearby.

We designed our tests to utilize every tool and function of each model. We carved white pine boards and maple branches. We opened bottles, cans, and shipping packaging. We disassembled and reassembled an old British carburetor, an electrical junction box, and a standard three-prong outlet.

We cut rope, twine, lamp wire, 14-gauge indoor branch circuit wire, maple saplings, branches, paper, and plastic. We also stripped the wires we cut and crimped electrical connectors. With the pliers, we gripped, squeezed, twisted, and turned various bits of hardware. Finally, we filed wood, metal, and even our own fingernails.

During these tests, we paid close attention to the performance of the tool in the given task, the ease of use, how each multitool ergonomically fit in our hand as we worked, and how we expect each tool to last over a long period of time. After all that was said and done, we noted our impressions to compile our final list.

For testing across the board, we evaluated each tool in common situations. For instance, the saw isn’t likely going to cut through 2x4s, so we opted for small branches, twine, and cardboard boxes.

#6245. An excavator found figurine molds at a Sudan temple in 1912 that was once a faience workshop

Digs at Sanam Temple in Sudan from 2018 to 2020 found a workshop from the mid-600s BC that made green figurines for Kush's royal tombs.

In 1912 the Egyptologist Francis Llewellyn Griffith dug at Sanam Temple, on the Nile in northern Sudan. His single season there lasted three months. He removed the fill on a light narrow-gauge Decauville railway.

Griffith also found clay molds for shabtis, the little figurines put in tombs. In 1922, however, he wrote only that they revealed one of the industries pursued in the temple.

He did not go looking for the place where that industry worked. Griffith did not systematically explore outside the walls, and he dumped his spoil heaps right up against them.

Excavations from 2018 to 2020 have now uncovered the faience workshop, behind the temple’s rear wall. It had three firing pits, two mudbrick basins and hundreds of beads, and it dates to the mid-seventh century BC. Some of its raw materials are still not identified with certainty.

King Taharqo ruled Kush and Egypt from about 690 to 664 BC. He founded the temple around 675 BC at Napata, his capital near the Fourth Cataract. He dedicated it to Amun-Bull-of-Nubia, a local form of the god.

A building known as the royal treasury stood nearby and held imported storage jars, finished goods and elephant tusks. The town grew up near Jebel Barkal, on land where shifts in the Nile created stable ground for a city.

Taharqo built all the way from the Nile delta to Napata. Much of his effort went to Karnak, where the oldest part of the temple sat on high ground among Nile channels. On the walls at Sanam is the Sanam Historical Inscription, the longest Kushite royal inscription that survives.

The new project’s first season lasted three weeks in January 2018. Kathryn Howley of New York University’s Institute of Fine Arts wrote it up in the first field report.

It also lists two rifle cartridges, probably from the late 19th century, by a wall the team suspects was Kitchener’s Fort, a colonial building Griffith took down.

Trench 3 was opened to the rear of the temple as a square of about 8 feet (2.5 meters). Below a lot of charcoal came faience beads, one intricately molded piece and wasters, lumps that went wrong in the firing.

Small shells and grinding stones lay with them. Workmen also picked up many beads on the surface around Griffith’s old spoil heaps.

In 2019 and 2020, workers from Karima and Merawi helped widen the trench to about 16 feet (5 meters) a side. Under the pits, the team then found a floor of broken storage jars. Someone had laid them flat to give a solid surface to work on.

The ash around the pits held hundreds of disk beads in blue, green and white, plus bits of faience vessels. Faience is mostly silica, with some alkali and lime. Simple ovens can reach the roughly 1,650 degrees Fahrenheit (900 degrees Celsius) needed to fire it.

One fragment, a broken green shabti, had no inscription on it. A new clay mold found inside the temple matches it exactly. Griffith’s older molds match shabtis George Reisner dug up at Nuri, the royal cemetery.

In Napatan Nubia only royalty used shabtis, while in Egypt people of many ranks had them. Egyptian cliff tombs still turn up burial goods, such as the pottery vessels and mirrors in rock-cut tombs of the south.

The paper calls Sanam “the first workshop securely identified for Kushite Nubia.” Egyptian marl jars with folded rims under the floor point to the eighth and seventh centuries BC. Red-slipped beakers fit the same range.

Faience paste needs lime. In Egypt it probably came from limestone, but most of Sudanese Nubia sits on the Nubian sandstone formation and has very little of it.

In 2018 Howley took the shells for Nile snails, which would have been easy to collect. She also noted that they were too small for anyone to gather just for food.

The new paper is by Rennan Lemos of Durham University’s Department of Archaeology, Howley and independent scholar Siobhan Shinn. Shadia Abdu Rabo of Sudan’s National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums co-wrote it.

The shells came out of the ash by the thousands. One bivalve is most likely Transkeia globosa, a Red Sea clam once called Diplodonta globosa.

Some snail shells still show traces of brown, and their shape fits both Nile snails of the family Hydrobiidae and marine Phasianellidae.

Workers broke the shells in the mudbrick basins with grindstones, which still carry the marks. Then they mixed the powder into the paste before firing.

Earlier Nubian potters had also put shell into their clay. Hauling so much shell from the coast was no small task. The authors argued that it took either direct control of distant communities or deals with desert groups who moved goods.

They described the shell-based recipe as a locally adapted version of an Egyptian craft. They also argued it served the production of objects for royal use.

Faience firing gives off smoke, and the smell depends on the fuel. In Egypt, workshops often made faience at the edge of a settlement, where the wind took the fumes off.

At Sanam, however, workers dug the pits immediately outside the temple’s sandstone wall. The authors read that placement as a sign that the temple controlled production, with some items meant only for royal use.

The 2020 season also turned up dark resin nuggets wedged between flagstones in the rear rooms. The team burned one lump as an experiment. It gave off a heavy, sweet smell like the bakhuur incense used in Sudan today, Howley wrote in her 2019-2020 report.

Shape alone could not settle the snail species. But the ongoing war in Sudan, the authors wrote, prevents further analysis. A mixed batch of Nile and Red Sea shells is still possible.

Nobody knows yet if real kilns stood over the pits. Collapsed mudbrick between pits 1 and 2 might be kiln walls. Then again, the workers might have used a cover they could lift off. The team dated the workshop by its pottery, and the paper gives no radiocarbon dates.

The authors think household workshops also made beads and pendants for ordinary people. Faience, after all, turns up in Sanam’s large non-elite cemetery. However, no one has yet fully investigated those other recipes with scientific methods.

New York University’s Institute of Fine Arts and the Egypt Exploration Society funded the fieldwork. An Explorers Club Rolex Grant and the Shelby White and Leon Levy Program paid too. Sudan’s antiquities corporation gave permission for the work, with help from its inspector, el-Hassan Ahmed.

Griffith wrote about his molds in 1922 without knowing where anyone had used them. Now, in Trench 3, the team has found the pits and the beads. It has also found a green shabti that fits a mold from inside the temple.

The full study was published in the journal Antiquity.

#6244. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#6243. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 14: Venus and Mercury in Virgo

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M.Sunset: 4:44 P.M.Moonrise: 11:33 A.M.Moonset: 8:56 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time on the 15th, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

#6242. Air pollution’s link to blood sugar has a surprising temperature twist

A European study links air pollution and temperature swings to higher blood sugar, offering clues to how environmental conditions may interact.

Air pollution is usually discussed as a threat to the lungs, while heat is treated as a seasonal health risk.

In a study of more than 21,000 Europeans without diabetes, particle pollution and temperature variability were linked to higher long-term blood sugar. The association with each depended on exposure to the other.

In modeled scenarios, reducing air pollution was associated with a larger drop in blood sugar under warmer, more variable conditions.

The study found no measurable association between residential greenery and blood sugar.

Nicole Probst-Hensch and her colleagues at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute and the University of Basel led the work.

Each person was measured once or a few times. So the study can show that pollution, temperature and blood sugar go together, not that one causes the other.

The team pooled nine long-running studies from Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain, the Czech Republic, Germany and Switzerland.

Together, they held 33,989 blood samples from 21,259 people, drawn between 1999 and 2021.

Ages ran from eight-year-olds in a Dutch birth cohort to the oldest adults in a Stockholm study.

The largest single group was 5,464 people from the GCAT study at the Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP) near Barcelona.

Each blood sample was tested for glycated hemoglobin, or HbA1c, which reflects average blood sugar over the previous two to three months.

Anyone with a diabetes diagnosis, diabetes medication or a reading in the diabetic range was left out, allowing the researchers to examine environmental associations in people without diabetes.

Each home address was then matched to a year of air pollution, greenery and temperature, from Europe-wide maps built by the EXPANSE project.

Of the three pollutants on the maps, only PM10 showed a consistent link to higher blood sugar.

PM10 includes airborne particles up to 10 micrometers across, including both fine and coarser particles. Nitrogen dioxide showed no consistent association, while the link with the finer PM2.5 was less consistent.

The other signal was how much the daily temperature swung over a year, more than the average temperature itself.

Their statistical method was built to find exposures that act together, and it did. Coarse particles and temperature swings interacted, so the effect of one depended on the level of the other.

The temperature-swing terms held up in nine of ten rounds of re-testing on different slices of the data.

One interaction, fine particles with average temperature, did not, and the authors treat it with caution.

Why would coarse particles matter for blood sugar? Larger particles get trapped in the upper airways, are moved up to the mouth and are swallowed, the authors wrote.

That fits other studies suggesting air pollution may alter gut bacteria.

The team then ran three futures through its model. The first cut coarse particles and nitrogen dioxide by 10 micrograms per cubic meter of air, and fine particles by 5.

These reductions were intended to approximate progress toward World Health Organization guideline levels. In the model, they were associated with lower blood sugar.

The second scenario raised the yearly average temperature by 0.9°F (0.5°C) and widened daily temperature swings by 1.8°F (1°C). The model associated these changes with higher blood sugar.

The third scenario combined cleaner air with warmer, more variable temperatures. Together, these changes were associated with a larger decrease in blood sugar than cleaner air alone.

The researchers expressed these modeled changes in standard deviations, a measure of how much blood sugar varied across the group.

Cleaner air alone was associated with a decrease of about 0.06 standard deviations, compared with about 0.07 under the combined scenario.

That is small for any one person. But most future diabetes comes from the many people at low or moderate risk, the authors wrote, so a small shift across a population matters.

The pattern was stronger in the 28,089 samples from nonsmokers and absent in the 5,900 from smokers.

Smoking causes inflammation of its own, the authors wrote, which may mask the effect.

Trees and parks are the usual prescription for a hot, polluted city. The study measured greenness around each home from satellite images, and the distance to the nearest green space.

Neither was linked to blood sugar, on its own or in combination with pollution or heat.

The links between pollution, temperature variability and blood sugar appeared almost exclusively in cities. In the less urban half of the samples, no stable link appeared.

The authors put that down to higher pollution and stronger heat islands in urban areas.

Natàlia Blay, a postdoctoral researcher at GCAT and a co-author, put the result in a wider frame.

“Including temperature in this approach is particularly relevant in the current context of climate change, where environmental exposures cannot be understood in isolation,” she said.

Diet and physical activity were not included in the models.

Participants had blood sugar measured once or a few times, so the study could not establish whether pollution caused higher blood sugar or whether other differences between people explained the association.

When the team split the group by body weight, the links disappeared in both halves.

The authors suggested that body fat might help explain the association, although this analysis could not establish its role.

The temperature maps began in 2003, so earlier blood samples were matched to later weather. HbA1c reflects only the three months before a blood draw, while the exposures were yearly averages.

Traffic noise, which other studies have tied to diabetes, had no Europe-wide map and was left out.

Whether cleaning the air of a hot city lowers its diabetes rate is the question the scenarios point at but can’t answer.

The authors wrote that noise belongs in the next round of this work, once Europe-wide noise maps exist.

The full study was published in the journal Environment International.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6240. A biologist who has helped name more than 55 frog species just added four more to his list, one with half-red eyes

Four new frog species from the Peruvian Andes raise the Oreobates genus from 27 to 31. One has a red-and-bronze iris and hides in holes under tree roots.

In July 2022, biologist Juan D. Valencia Málaga collected seven small brown frogs of a still unnamed species on the forest floor near Canaan, a village in Peru’s San Martín department, at about 6,900 feet (2,100 meters).

Their eyes were red on top and greenish bronze below. All of them were caught next to holes under raised roots, and they ducked into those holes when threatened.

The Canaan frog is now one of four new frog species in the genus Oreobates.

It was described by a team based in Peru and the United States that includes Alessandro Catenazzi of Florida International University, who has helped describe more than 55 frog species.

Each of the four is known from one or two places, and the paper gives no population counts.

The paper, led by Pablo J. Venegas of Rainforest Partnership and the Instituto Peruano de Herpetología in Lima, raises the genus from 27 to 31 species. The six authors also include James W. Ttito, Luis A. García-Ayachi, Michael Gulman and Juan D. Valencia.

The frogs came from rapid surveys in the departments of San Martín and Huánuco between 2018 and 2025. The team walked slowly along streams and through the forest with headlamps, from 7 p.m. to 3 a.m., and caught the frogs by hand.

The specimens now sit in the herpetology collection of CORBIDI, the Centro de Ornitología y Biodiversidad in Lima.

Like all their relatives in the Terrarana group, these frogs breed on land and skip the tadpole stage, as do three other frogs that develop without tadpoles.

Its name, Oreobates foliaspectrum, joins the Latin for leaf and apparition. Red eyes, long toes and mottled color led the authors to compare it to a ghostly image in the leaf litter.

The female holotype, the specimen that anchors the name, measures 1.3 inches (32.4 millimeters) from snout to vent.

The forest at Canaan is a patch of low trees under 20 feet (6 meters) tall, with tree ferns and Chusquea bamboo on poor sandy soil. The patch sits in a matrix of cattle pastures, and the authors saw signs of frequent trampling by cattle on the forest floor.

In an October 30, 2026 article from his university, Catenazzi described how the team tells one frog from the next, by traits such as “this one is black, this one is brown, this one has a little tubercle, this one has smooth skin, and so on.”

Valencia did the Canaan fieldwork with companions including Benoît Segerer and Fabrice Schmitt, and he stayed with Artemio Chávez and his wife Francelit Espejo in the village.

Oreobates nigrumcompletum, Latin for entirely black, is deep brown to nearly black above and below. Ttito and Gulman found it at Finca Oso Pecho Blanco, a farm in the Uchiza district of San Martín, between July 30 and August 4, 2025, at 3,790 to 5,545 feet (1,155 to 1,690 meters).

The farm’s owner, Jorge Díaz Cotrina, guided them. This species has a dark iris flecked with gold.

The same two biologists collected Oreobates azulensis in July 2025 in the Azpusana Valley, in the Pucuyacu district of Huánuco.

The site lies in the buffer zone of Cordillera Azul National Park, and the name refers to that mountain range. The males measure 0.8 to 0.9 inches (20 to 23 millimeters), and all specimens have copper irises.

Oreobates chirimoto is named after Nuevo Chirimoto, a settlement in the upper basin of the Huayabamba River. García-Ayachi and field assistant Juan Gamboa collected three specimens there on December 13, 2018, at about 6,370 feet (1,942 meters), with local guide Francisco Galoc.

All three were in leaf litter between 8 and 11 p.m. on a steep slope cut by blackwater streams. The species has a yellow belly and orange groin and thighs.

APECO, a Peruvian conservation group, paid for that trip with a Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund grant for work on an endemic harlequin frog.

Money for the Cordillera Azul survey came from CIMA Cordillera Azul, and a 2024 Carlos Ponce del Prado award paid for the Oso Pecho Blanco work.

The team extracted DNA from nine specimens and sent the amplified pieces of five genes to MCLAB, a lab in San Francisco, for sequencing.

The team set those against sequences of 42 other specimens from the public GenBank database, in an alignment 3,538 DNA letters long.

The resulting family tree, the most complete so far for the genus, placed O. azulensis, O. foliaspectrum and O. nigrumcompletum in one northern Peruvian group. O. chirimoto landed in a different branch, near species from southern Peru.

O. azulensis differs by only 2 percent in one mitochondrial gene from its closest relative, O. shunkusacha. The authors kept it separate because the two have different skin texture, with pointed, uneven granules in the new species.

According to Catenazzi, describing a frog also means checking old type specimens, the original reference animals, at the British Museum, other European museums, New York or the Smithsonian.

Many were described in the 19th or 20th century, and seeing them means “going to all those places and actually handling them,” he said.

All four frogs live in the Peruvian Yungas, the humid forests on the eastern slope of the Andes, between about 3,800 and 6,900 feet (1,155 and 2,100 meters).

The authors suggest that deep dry valleys may act as barriers for these frogs. The Marañón Valley separates the central Andes of Peru from the northern Andes, and on the eastern slopes of the northern Andes only one Oreobates species, O. quixensis, occurs, apparently spilling over from the Amazon lowlands.

Catenazzi’s lab at Florida International University is also studying two other frog species whose skin peptides have antimicrobial, wound-healing and antifungal properties. Similar work on frog skin compounds as a source of new antibiotics is under way in other labs.

Other recent descriptions from the country include three new frog species from Peru with an uncertain future.

The university article says the team uses calls along with body traits and DNA to separate species. The paper itself rests on morphology, color and genes, and it contains no call recordings.

All four new species lack vocal slits, openings in the mouth linked to the calls males use to attract females. The authors wrote that bioacoustic and behavioral studies are needed to find out why.

The support for the position of O. chirimoto on the family tree is low, at 59 out of 100, and the role of the river valleys as barriers needs wider sampling. O. chirimoto is known from three specimens, and O. foliaspectrum from a single forest patch at Canaan.

The paper gives no threat assessment for any of the four. At Canaan, O. foliaspectrum still hides among the roots of a small forest surrounded by pasture.

The full study was published in the journal Diversity.

#6238. Nov. 14, 2012: NASA announces an extended mission for Kepler

The Kepler Space Telescope, launched March 6, 2009, was designed to search the Milky Way for exoplanets. Using the transit method, Kepler ultimately observed over 500,00 stars and contributed to the discovery of almost 2,700 exoplanets.

Though Kepler was originally intended for a 3.5-year mission, NASA announced on Nov. 14, 2012, that the space telescope had successfully completed its primary mission and would be embarking on an extended mission. When a second gyroscope (also referred to as a reaction wheel) failed in May 2013 – the first having failed in July 2012 – that mission was in question, however, as it left the spacecraft with limited control for pointing. But engineers were able to craft a workaround using the momentum of the Sun’s light pressure to keep Kepler evenly and steadily directed, and the extended mission using this methodology, dubbed K2, was formally approved in May 2014. Kepler continued to function for a further four years, and was retired in October 2018 when it ran out of fuel. TESS (the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) has since inherited its planet-hunting mantle.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6237. A South African dig shows early humans were already showing signs of advanced, complex thinking 60,000 years ago

60,000-year-old red ochre from a South African cave revealed hidden antelope proteins, proving early humans intentionally mixed animal parts into their ancient recipes.

It is a 60,000-year-old cold case that scientists finally solved using modern technology. By hunting for ancient proteins hidden in a patch of red dirt, researchers discovered that early humans deliberately mixed crushed clay with the remains of a massive African antelope.

This proves that modern science can now unlock the exact recipes used by humans in the Stone Age.

Between 2011 and 2013, archaeologists at Klipdrift Shelter in South Africa dug through a thin red ochre surface that may have been over 3 feet (1 meter) long. The shelter sits in the coastal cliffs of De Hoop Nature Reserve.

Bits of it were bagged and archived at the University of the Witwatersrand‘s satellite lab in Cape Town.

Years later Zahra Haghighi of the University of Bergen in Norway pulled five of those bags for protein analysis. Two held collagen from a common eland, a large antelope native to southern Africa.

The layer is about 60,000 years old. Haghighi’s team reads the result as eland material mixed with ochre powder on purpose, or as an ochre-treated eland hide left at the site. Two positive samples are not enough to pick between them.

Klipdrift Shelter is about 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Cape Town. It is one of three sites of the Klipdrift Complex, with Klipdrift Cave and Klipdrift Cave Lower.

Bergen’s SFF Centre for Early Sapiens Behaviour (SapienCE) lists the complex among the sites its team has exclusive access to. Crews excavated there in 2011, 2012, 2013 and 2018.

Single-grain luminescence dates the shelter’s 23 Middle Stone Age units to between about 52,000 years ago at the top and 72,000 at the bottom. Out came stone tools, marine shells, animal bones, hearths, engraved ostrich eggshell and 597 pieces of ochre.

Layer PBE, one of the dig’s numbered sediment layers, where the red surface lay, is part of the Howiesons Poort, a stone tool phase of southern Africa.

Patches of ochre powder of various sizes turned up all through those layers. This one was exceptional, possibly 16 inches (40 centimeters) wide, with surviving pieces 5 to 7 millimeters thick.

Its precise extent was not documented during the dig, and the surface was taken out entirely in 2011 to 2013. The size estimate therefore comes from site notes and from photographs, some of them by Magnus Haaland and Ole Unhammer.

Haghighi, first author of the paper, chose five archived samples from layers PBD, PBE, PCA and PBA-PBB, weighing 30 to 150 milligrams each.

None had been collected with protein work in mind. The export permits came from Heritage Western Cape and the South African Heritage Resources Agency.

Her co-authors include Takumi Tsutaya of Kyushu University in Japan and Enrico Cappellini of the University of Copenhagen. Sediment does not give up proteins the way bone does, so the group devised a method it calls AB (acid and base) digestion.

Two samples of about 130 milligrams sat in a guanidine buffer at 99°C (210°F) for 10 minutes. Then came hydrochloric acid overnight at 4°C (39°F), and then sodium hydroxide. Enzymes then chopped up whatever protein had come loose.

That screen turned up mammal collagen. A second extraction with strong acid and no enzyme followed on all five samples.

The peptides were read on an Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer. The search used 711 mammal collagen sequences plus those of 44 African bovid species.

Collagen was confidently identified in two of the five, one sample from PBE and one from PBD, which sits right above it.

The COL1A1 chain, one of the two protein chains that make up type I collagen, matched several African bovids, the cattle-and-antelope family. Fragments of the COL1A2 chain matched one species alone, the common eland, Taurotragus oryx.

Sixty-nine peptides were identified, adding up to 171 amino acids or 16.5 percent of COL1A2. A proline at position 693, a serine at 720 and a threonine at 878 occur in eland only. The 720 and 878 sites were picked up in both layers, in at least three spectra apiece.

The giant eland, the other member of the genus, now lives in central Africa and has no published collagen sequence. The authors assumed the two species kept their present ranges 60,000 years ago.

Nearly every asparagine and glutamine, two of the amino acids in the peptides, had deamidated, a chemical change that builds up over long spans of time.

The paper suggests iron in the ochre may have helped the collagen last. The oldest ancient DNA recovered in Africa is about 18,000 years old. Older material calls for protein work, as with the ancient proteins pulled from Homo naledi fossils in South Africa.

Stray eland bone in the sediment would also leave collagen. So 15 samples went under optical microscopes, and some under a Zeiss Supra 55VP scanning electron microscope at the University of Bergen’s ELMILAB.

Only four of the 15 had anything resembling bone, one or two fragments apiece, none over about 0.1 inch (3 millimeters). Three of those four were from PBD, and PBE had none at all.

A thin section of the PBE surface mixed rounded ochre particles of around 1 micrometer with fragments of 2 to 5 millimeters.

That range, plus the quantity of ochre needed, supports the authors’ view that people formed the feature. They described the eland collagen as “most probably due to human action.”

Earlier work on the shelter’s animal bones had already identified eland among the remains.

The paper offers two scenarios. Either eland protein went into an ochre mixture that became part of the surface, or an ochre-coated eland hide was left in the shelter. In the second case the hide decayed and its ochre stayed in place.

Elsewhere in South Africa, two abalone shells at Blombos Cave, along the same coast, held an ochre-rich compound around 100,000 years old. At Sibudu, milk proteins on a stone flake pointed to a paint of ochre and milk about 49,000 years old.

Ochre has been linked to hafting glue, hide work, medicine and sunscreen. Sunscreen comes up in research on how Homo sapiens coped with intense UV light.

In an October 21 release, Kyushu University said evidence of organic components mixed with ochre had been “extremely rare, especially in Africa.”

All of this hangs on two of five small samples from a single feature at a single site. Which eland tissue the collagen came from is not known. The authors wrote that working it out would need a database built to tell tissues apart.

Eland are revered in San mythology, the paper notes, yet the authors called this one case “not sufficient to support the ritual significance of eland” in the Middle Stone Age.

They want the work repeated at other sites from that period. In Senegal, Middle Stone Age tools stayed in use 20,000 years longer than once thought.

The mass spectrometry data are in the PRIDE archive under PXD069507. The red surface in layer PBE no longer exists at Klipdrift. What is left of it is a handful of small bags of sediment in Cape Town, and two of them held the eland.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6236. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”
