Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria.

According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus, repeated that story without question.

But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die?

Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery.

"We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones, a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email.

What historians largely agree on is that Cleopatra VII, the last queen of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, took her own life and that she chose a method that left her body composed and dignified.

Physical evidence of Cleopatra's death is elusive. Much of Alexandria's royal quarter now lies underwater, and underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, who has been excavating it, hasn't found the queen's mausoleum, Jones said. Even if Cleopatra's remains surfaced, bones would be unlikely to show evidence of snake venom, she added, noting that forensics is outside her area of expertise.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Divers celebrate as a crane pulls an artifact from the waters at Abu Qir bay in Alexandria, Egypt on Aug. 21, 2025.

The best witness may have been Olympus, Cleopatra's personal physician. "Unfortunately, nothing survives of Olympus' account," Jones said.

What does remain is a story told largely by Cleopatra's enemies. The earliest surviving account is a poem by the Roman poet Horace, whose patron was a close friend of Octavian, said Jane Draycott, a historian at the University of Glasgow. His Ode 1.37, written around the time of her death, celebrates Octavian's victory and already pictures the queen handling serpents — yet it ends with grudging admiration for a woman who refused to be paraded as a trophy.

Following her capture, Cleopatra was held under military guard. By then, she had already tried to end her life twice. Cleopatra had tried to stab herself when Roman soldiers broke into the mausoleum where she had barricaded herself, and she later tried to starve herself, stopping only after Octavian threatened her children.

To Draycott, those attempts leave little doubt that Cleopatra would rather die than live as a captive. "She does not want to be a prisoner; she does not want to be led through the streets of Rome in triumph as a defeated foe," she told Live Science.

In the Greco-Roman world, suicide didn't carry the stigma it later acquired under Christianity, she added. "It was a way of wiping the slate clean, removing any shame, any disgrace from yourself." After the defeat of his remaining forces at Alexandria and hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony was the first of the two lovers to die by suicide.

According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, who based his account on that of Cleopatra's personal physician, Cleopatra visited Antony's tomb, bathed, ate and sent Octavian a sealed letter asking to be buried beside Antony, signaling that she meant to die. Octavian realized what was happening and sent messengers rushing to her, but they arrived too late. They found her dead in her royal regalia, with her attendants Iras and Charmion dying beside her.

A statue depicting Cleopatra's suicide by asp, the most famous of several ancient theories.

Jones has compiled what ancient historians, biographers, geographers and physicians wrote about Cleopatra's death. Every source mentions a snakebite, but several also suggest other possibilities, including a poisonous ointment, poison hidden in a hollow hairpin, and snake venom poured into a wound the queen made by biting herself. Only one of these writers, the geographer Strabo, was alive when Cleopatra died, and the only people in the room with her died, too.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio wrote that the sole clue was a pair of faint pricks on her arm. That doesn't settle much, however. "A cobra bite can appear as two small puncture wounds, but not all cobra bites appear this way and not all double puncture wounds result from snakebites," Jones said.

Jones traces the snake version of the story to Octavian, who was in Alexandria when Cleopatra died. Plutarch reported that an image of Cleopatra with an asp clinging to her was carried in Octavian's triumphal procession in Rome. "Octavian, however, was Cleopatra's enemy and for that reason we may not want to accept his account uncritically," Jones said.

Draycott suggested another possible source of confusion: Snake-shaped jewelry was fashionable in Alexandria at the time, so Romans viewing an effigy of the queen may have mistaken a snake bracelet for a real snake.

Draycott doesn't think one snake could have killed all three women. Jones is less certain. Snakes don't inject the same amount of venom with every bite, and some "dry bites" deliver none at all, Jones said. "On the other hand, I don't think it is impossible, as the body of a cobra contains enough venom to kill multiple people," she added.

The general view among historians, Draycott said, is that Cleopatra took some kind of poison — one that worked quickly and didn't cause seizures or vomiting. The absence of these symptoms is telling: An asp is believed to be what is now known as the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), whose venom causes a slow, agonizing death with respiratory failure.

A young Egyptian cobra (Naja haja) strikes a typical defensive pose in scrubland near Sidi Ifni, Morocco.

Cleopatra likely would have had other means, then. Alexandria was the Mediterranean's center of scientific study, and texts from the period, such as Nicander's "Theriaca," catalog venomous animals, Jones noted. Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, even consulted the pharmacologist Zopyrus about antidotes. Plutarch claimed that Cleopatra personally oversaw experiments that observed the effects of deadly poisons on condemned prisoners.

Still, that claim and other poison stories should be read with caution, Draycott said, because they draw on Roman stereotypes about women. In the Roman view, "manly men will battle with swords," while women, seen as "deceitful and weak" at this time, were thought to kill in secret. "They'll sneak it into your food," Draycott said, summing up the stereotype.

Roman writers were equally suspicious. Poisoning allegations dogged the Hellenistic dynasties of ancient Egypt and the neighboring Seleucid kingdom, as well as Rome's own imperial family. Some were probably true, Draycott said, but others may have been foodborne illnesses or other health conditions people didn't understand.

The method may remain a mystery, but for most historians, the motive doesn't change: Cleopatra chose to die on her own terms.

#6224. APOD: 2026 November 12 – Moon, Venus and Spica Meet

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: Not all those who wander are lost. A night sky example is that planets wander, and in fact the very word "planet" comes from "wandering star" in Greek. As planets shift relative to fixed stars, they may appear from our perspective to get closer to other astronomical objects. Such meetings are called conjunctions. They don't happen by chance, but follow the precise laws of celestial mechanics. This peaceful image, captured in Poland, shows the crescent Moon above the Tatra Mountains, and bright Venus close by, a little lower in the horizon. The bright star to the left of Venus is Spica in the constellation of Virgo, the Maiden. Spica is one of the brightest stars in the sky, only about 250 light-years away. It was found in 1890 that Spica is a binary star: two massive blue stars orbiting each other every 4 days. But earlier this year it was reported that Spica, the current companion of wandering Venus, is actually a triple system.Tomorrow's picture: what's next?

#6223. 14 Best Steakhouses in New York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini

No single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC. Each has its strengths, and some are certainly better than others. There are the classics—Keens and Gallaghers in Midtown, Delmonico's in the Financial District, Peter Luger over in Williamsburg—that have been here for a hundred years or more, and for good reason. They are dimly-lit, tavern-like, with walls clad in wood. The menus do not change. The new and newish guard variously emulate and do their own thing. Increasingly, we are seeing steakhouses taking the basic assignment—red meat and sides in a formal dining room—and running with it in various cultural directions. Below, we've rounded up our favorites across this board. What's most important is their shared ability to make its diner feel important, a feat that goes beyond (but does require) the ability to gorge on good steak.

Read our complete New York City guide here, which includes:

Seagram Building, 99 E 52nd St, Midtown Manhattan

I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel important. No place has succeeded so impeccably in this mission as The Grill, where I was whisked from a downstairs lobby into the glamorous dining room as though a visiting board member come to town to be courted and impressed. I went for lunch, so the metal chain curtains that undulate (yes, they are ever-moving) over the massive windows shimmered in the daylight. Everyone except for me, it seemed, as there on very important business. I was the only male diner that I could see not in a jacket. The menu is very spendy (you cannot get a cocktail for less than $26) and therefore especially reserved for special occasions. Peppered filet mignon and martini, I'd say, are the way to go, but if it's lunch and the prime rib roast beef sandwich is being served, it's a worthy detour. —C.H.

The best thing that happened to me at 4 Charles Prime Rib was that I made a new friend. Steak and martinis and burgers, they're all fabulous—make no mistake. But sometimes it’s the life that comes at you in pursuit of those delicious menu items that leaves you feeling the most full. Too corny? Allow me to elaborate.

4 Charles is one of the toughest tables in town. Like Torrisi, it’s practically a private members' club where the only people who can land a reservation are those who’ve eaten there before. Hopeful walk-ins start lining up over an hour before opening at 4 p.m., and I got there at 2:45 p.m. to find myself second in line. I sat on the West Village townhouse stoop and enjoyed the day, enjoyed the sight of the staff puttering around setting up, glared at the people with reservations who we in line agreed were “line cutters.” When the host began seating people around 3:45 p.m., she told me that I was the first single walk-in and would therefore enjoy the one table by the door that they reserve for such parties. The man behind me, who arrived nary five minutes after I did, was told he would therefore have to wait until I was done. “Can’t I just sit with him?” he asked in earnest bewilderment. “Sure!” I responded.

And so together we unhinged our jaws and ate the 10-ounce double wagyu smash burger with thick slabs of bacon, his with an egg, and together we poured the beef jus over the pink center of the titular 4 Charles Cut and expressed our unexpected delight with the horseradish cream accoutrement. Together we drank martinis—I, a perfect vesper; he, an espresso; and then a chocolate each. If you’re going to try to go, I recommend you do so in this way. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Peter Luger isn't just the Brooklyn steakhouse. It just might be the New York City steakhouse, especially if history carries any weight with you, dear reader. This fine establishment has sat at the same address in the Williamsburg Bridge's shadow since 1887, and the interiors carry about as many frills as your average public house—dark wood, plaster walls, and so on. The menu is just as unadorned, with the most popular menu items being the dry-aged steak for two, steak for three, or steak for four. You can also, rest assured, get a single steak, lamb chops, salmon, or filet of sole. The Luger's sizzling bacon is not to be missed, nor are the sliced tomatoes and onions with Luger's Own sauce (pro tip: they go quite well together.) If you're there before 3:45 p.m., you'd also be wise to order the over-½-lb Luger burger, which is so simple and bloody with optional American cheese that your eyes will roll back in your head. —C.H.

This summer, the Montecito and Malibu staple Lucky's Steakhouse came to roost on a bustling street in New York’s Soho—and has been a fun addition to the city’s oft-stodgy steakhouse landscape ever since. Importantly, it’s a cool counterpoint—with its intimate size, Jazz Age-y murals, sexy date-night vibe, and a menu that accommodates non-steak eaters (i.e. me, a pescatarian). I know what you’re thinking: Why is a non-meat eater reviewing Lucky’s? Well, precisely for the fact that steakhouses can be wincingly non-inclusive, despite often being the restaurant of choice on special occasions. And Lucky’s feels different, not least because of its ambience. On a recent night, we started with the oysters, the peaky-toe crab cocktail, house chips, and Jimmy’s Greek salad (named after a family member of the owner). I then got the salmon, initially a perverse choice—because it usually plays poor country cousin at most steakhouses—but it was excellent. And we really dug into the sides—onion rings, market vegetables, and creamed corn. Both times I ate there, my companions ordered the 10-oz Gene’s Filet and I heard murmurs of firm approval. Whatever your dietary preference, don’t miss Lucky’s martini service, for which multiple servers will shake (or stir) your drinks table-side and in unison—because a little theatre hurts no one.

Head 10 blocks south of New York’s Koreatown (see an itinerary of the neighborhood here), and you'll find Cote, a Korean steakhouse and one of the city’s best and buzziest restaurants. There’s no shortage of a la carte options, but the prix-fixe Butcher’s Feast is where diners should start. For $74 a person, you're treated to seasonal ban-chan, savory egg soufflé, two stews (including spicy kimchi stew), and the house selection of beef, including USDA Prime and Wagyu, cooked on the table with smokeless grills. The restaurant’s award-winning wine list features an impressive Champagne selection, and all by-the-glass pours come from Magnums, the large-format bottles that sommeliers say keeps wines younger and fresher. There's also a second location at 550 Madison that's a bit grander, should that suit you. —D.F.

Gallaghers is the best steakhouse to eat at before a Broadway show. Wood paneled walls covered in framed old photographs (one of singer Perry Comon had to be labeled “this is not Jeffrey Epstein” due to those two men’s shared resemblance) offset the inhumane Midtown environment just beyond the front door. This is a place that’s as good for steak (and it really is good for steak) as it is for all of the accoutrements one expects of a good steakhouse—beyond the bovine, highlights include the old fashioned, the creamed spinach, the house-smoked bacon, and the beautifully browned veal chop parmigiana. Putting it all over the edge is the people watching—real live businesspeople drowning their sorrows at the bar alongside the theatergoers, and haughty waiters doing buttoned-up to the max. —C.H.

The only difficult choice to make when entering Keens is where to look first. Is it up, at the 90,000 pipes lining the ceiling? To the glass cases, where the most famous churchwardens—15-inch pipes—smoked by the likes of Babe Ruth and General MacArthur are stored? In the bar, are you mesmerized by the Miss Keen painting (a nude, lounging on her bear rug) right away, or are you too distracted by the New-York-ad-men-in-the-'50s vibe? This steakhouse, open since 1883, delivers something new to look at every time you go. Keens was originally called a chop house, in recognition of its famous mutton chop, and although that is good and musty and intense, most people are ordering steak. There’s the porterhouse for two or three, the chateaubriand, and the filet mignon—which is actually fabulous here. You want the béarnaise or au poivre sauce on the side, and the creamed spinach, which is less a vegetable than it is dessert. There's also the matter of the burger, which can be ordered up to the dining room from the more casual bar menu. —Alex Van Buren

1271 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan

From the moment you walk into Cuerno, there's a sense of importance—the crowd, in suits and slicked back hair, is well-dressed; the dining room is always bustling and full, necks turning to see who else has walked in; and tableside preparations are happening left and right. This is Northern Mexican meat at its finest, in a space that feels true to that spirit—big leather booths, a colorful tile mural of a skeleton riding a bull—and with a menu that won't let you down. There are expected starters, like fresh guac and queso fundido, but also a chicarrón de pulpo bursting with flavor, and a charcoal-roasted cauliflower complemented by truffle and habanero. The main event, of course, are the steaks, like the decadent Taco Taquero with perfect skirt steak, and fire-roasted bone marrow scooped onto each tortilla tableside, or the Norteño-style arrachera served with chiltepin butter and avocado salsa.

Portions are generous, so come in a group of four people minimum to actually try different sections of the menu. And though most steakhouses focus on wine (and the wine list is good here), I like the chance to pair smoky mezcal and tequila cocktails with the heavier food. —Megan Spurrell

355 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg, Brooklyn

Not just in Williamsburg, not just in New York City, but truly one of the coziest, best-value steakhouses I’ve ever been to, St. Anselm manages a rare balance: laid-back yet elevated, intimate without trying too hard, and consistently delicious. The space feels like a hidden tavern—dark wood, low light, and just enough buzz and energy to make it feel like a special night out. The Butcher’s Steak is the standout—charred to perfection, tender and juicy inside, and ideal for sharing (for two) alongside fingerling potatoes and long green beans. Go for a group lunch or, better yet, settle in after dark when the candles are lit and the place feels like a warm, secret pocket of the city. Ask your server—or better yet, belly up to the bar—and you’ll get a wine recommendation that pairs not just with the food, but with your mood. —Jessica Chapel

513 E 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan

Buenos Aires earns major points for nostalgia: The tiny dining room is adorned in hanging soccer jerseys, televisions showing live games and commentary, and scarfs and pendants for teams like the Boca Juniors. There are couples on dates, families with kids, and even, in my case, a dude who came in alone and ordered his regular with his headphones in. (Ask about celebrities and they'll bring out an iPad with photos of grinning staff beside countless Latin America soccer players, American actors, and even Matt Damon who apparently hosted two birthday parties here in the early 2000s.) All to say, this isn't the place to bring the corporate account or close the deal, but it is the place to roll up your sleeves and tuck into a massive skirt steak, expertly cooked, and served no-frills—just a great piece of meat on a plate. Do save room for the empanadas (carne cortada a cuchillo, of course); on my next visit, I'm planning to order the sweetbreads as well. —M.S.

Glam, glam, glam with a capital G. Golden Steer's New York iteration—the original is in Vegas, and little of that location's trademark opulence has been sacrificed in adapting the brand for New York. We're not in Midtown either, but in the West Village, and this is a fitting addition to that neighborhood as it increasingly wears its wealth on its sleeve. Entering this crimson bunker is a cinematic experience—long hallways flanked by side quests like the capacious but moody bar. What to get? Sink into your plush booth and go full Sin City: the bloody bull oyster shooter (where a rich beef broth-spiked shot of bloody mary chases the slime), the big ole baked potato, and a Caesar dotingly mixed tableside. Any cut of meat will do. —C.H.

56 Beaver St, Financial District, Manhattan

The definitive downtown steakhouse is also New York City's oldest. Its home since 1837 is 56 Beaver Street, a dramatic triangular lot at the intersection of Beaver, William, and South William in the Financial District. When I visited on a mid-May evening, the exterior was bedecked in American regalia—they were to film an episode of The Gilded Age there the next day (the new season is currently airing on HBO) depicting the ticker tape parade welcoming the Statue of Liberty to the city. All of this history would be moot were the steakhouse inside not very good, which it is from top to bottom—superlative, doting service in the mural-clad dining room, stiff drinks, perfect cuts of meat. As with every steakhouse, there are a couple of signature items beyond steak that you should consider. Here, it's wedge salad and buttery Lobster Newberg, said to have been invented there. Don't miss either, but steak is still the thing, namely the titular flagship cut—a glistening 18-ounce ribeye that stands alone on the plate, needing no accoutrements. —Charlie Hobbs

Dinner and a show in New York City’s midtown sounds fabulous, but in practice usually means settling for a meal that delivers more on convenience than cuisine or atmosphere. Carvesteak, a newish steakhouse on the west side of 48th street, stepped up to all these qualities after I saw The Rocky Horror Show earlier this year. Designed by David Rockwell and the Rockwell Group, it’s moody, mirrored interiors are filled with little nods to the Broadway history it shoulders—including a dramatic velvet curtain that the bartender at the martini bar told me was once part of the set for Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera (even if untrue, it certainly looked the part). Speaking of the martini bar, it’s not to be missed: a pocket-sized station to post yourself up at before or after dinner. Food-wise, this is a classic steakhouse menu, but with a little bit of flashiness thanks to the restaurant’s Las Vegas origins (it debuted at Resorts World Las Vegas in 2021): think, prime cuts and aged rib eyes with all the sides and sauces you would expect, but also the option to order a potato and caviar “popsicle.” There’s a pre-theater menu, too, but for the full experience I suggest coming hungry and catching the last call before 10 p.m. —Lale Arikoglu

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6222. The 8 Best Portable Refrigerators If You’re Tired of Buying Bags of Ice

This convenient appliance works better than your average cooler and offers versatile power options. Here are the ones we recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Even the best coolers we’ve tested from names like Yeti, Coleman, and RTIC with superior insulation eventually get too warm for ice to stay frozen. That’s where portable refrigerators shine, offering cooling capability that you just can’t get from a regular cooler. They’re great for long camping trips where you need to keep meat and other food at safe temperatures and come in plenty of sizes to suit hardcore camper rigs and RVs or fit in a standard sedan.

Portable refrigerators—often called car refrigerators—plug into your car’s 12-volt outlet, an AC outlet, or a portable power station. They’re pricier and heavier than the standard cooler, but they're more efficient at cooling. And you get to skip the expense and hassle of dealing with bags of ice. They can also be helpful around the house if your fridge breaks or there’s a power outage.

We used our expertise on coolers, power stations, and camping gear to find the best portable refrigerators. We checked camping and overlanding gear reviews and forums to find models that hold up on long treks in remote areas and are viable alternatives for people who don't want to deal with bags of ice for a cooler.

We chose options in different capacities and across a range of prices and prioritized models that offer convenient features like USB chargers, wheels, and LED lights. If you want some extra cooling power on-the-go, consider one of the portable refrigerators for your next trek.

This portable fridge from Bodega has great build quality, convenient features for easy portability, and cools down fast. The compressor can cool the interior down to 32 degrees Fahrenheit in about 30 minutes.

It has two separate compartments to keep things organized. They can’t be individually controlled but the smaller section typically gets cooler than the larger side. It also has a user-friendly app for setting the temperature and a USB port to charge other devices. Some customers report minor differences between the temperature they see on the app versus the actual internal temperature, but say it’s only off by a couple degrees.

The portable refrigerator has sturdy handles and a built-in LED light so you can quickly find what you need in the dark. Standout features include wheels and a drain plug—two things that are standard on most larger coolers but something a lot of portable fridges lack. The lid can be opened from either side or popped off entirely for fast loading.

This portable refrigerator is a great value for efficient cooling, a low power draw, and large capacity. The 59-quart space is split into two zones for easy organizing and the unit comes with a removable wire basket.

Its tall, slender shape fits easily behind a row of seats in the car. The handles are also removable to make for easy stowing. The app lets you set and monitor temps, though you can’t do much else. Some users report the app is user-friendly but wish it had more features.

The Alpicool is a budget portable refrigerator that cools down fast to roughly zero degrees Fahrenheit and operates quietly in comparison to most other models.

It has an automatic shutoff to ensure it doesn’t drain your car or portable battery and eco mode that pulls less energy. An external LCD display and control panel shows you the interior temperature. This budget option also has an LED light inside and a drain plug.

Setup is rather easy but the included manual doesn’t show you how to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit. The brand’s website has a detailed owner’s manual that's more helpful.

Thinking of Igloo might still conjure the image of the old-school Playmate cooler you had as a kid. But the ICF electric cooler is anything but that. The portable refrigerator has a sturdy plastic build that can handle the bumps and bruises that come with transporting it to sporting events, grocery stores, and campgrounds.

Its spacious interior works as one large storage space or, with the help of the included removable divider, two separate areas. This helps separate dry items like canned drinks from wet items like fruit and sandwiches. The ICF is also remarkably simple. All the controls are built right onto the body, so all you have to do is turn it on and set the temperature.

Like other portable refrigerators, the ICF has a three-stage battery protection system to prevent it from draining your car battery.

The Bouge comes in a compact package that can serve as a personal cooler for a remote overnight, or extra storage on long treks. It has a single compartment that works as a fridge or freezer.

Set the temperature from the external control panel and monitor through the LCD thermometer. There’s no app to keep tabs on the temperature while driving but customers report it stays consistent even in hotter ambient temps. Recessed handles add to its space-saving design.

Some reviews mention the external thermometer can be off as much as seven degrees—a bit higher than most other models.

The Travoca Rigel eCooler has a number of small, but notable, features that intrigued us right away. For one, it’s somewhat modular. You can unscrew the wood paneling on the front and replace it with attachments such as a small shelf for placing drinks or snacks.

The lid is fully detachable and reversible, so you can pop the whole thing off and get a full look at everything inside. Beyond this, dual-zone cooling is powerful. Each section can work as either a fridge or freezer.

And if you don’t need separate sections, the internal divider comes out, converting the entire interior to one large space at the same temperature. Travoca also sells internal baskets separately for easier organization.

Dometic is the best-known brand of portable refrigerators, with a reputation for turning out models that are durable and reliable With that comes the higher price tag, but overlanders and outdoor enthusiasts are still fans—I see this one touted most in forums as the main fridge people use while traveling on long remote treks.

It’s on the heavier side at 60 pounds when empty, but its compressor is more powerful than other models on this list—and it operates quietly.

The portable refrigerator has a sleek display and an intuitive app to set and keep tabs on the interior temperature, plus a USB port for charging for mobile devices.

With a wheeled base and telescopic handles, this portable fridge from BougeRV is a well-built mix between portability and size. The interior comes with two separate sections. You can tune each to different temperatures, allowing you to have both a functional fridge and freezer at the same time.

One of the more user-friendly features the CRD2 has is an opening for a standalone battery. While sold separately, the battery allows the cooler to operate without any large power source, like a wall outlet or car, nearby. With the attached battery, the portable fridge can run for up to 20 hours with no other power source, making it an ideal way to escape to the beach or sleep overnight in the woods away from your car and still wake up to fresh produce and unspoiled milk.

Portable refrigerators run on a compressor just like your kitchen fridge and freezer and keep food fresher a lot longer than a cooler and ice. Most reach an average minimum temperature of -4 to -7 degrees Fahrenheit to freeze and refrigerate food, though some are refrigerators only, reaching a minimum temperature of 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

Although portable refrigerators don't rely solely on insulation for cooling power, they're still well insulated enough to take some of the load off the compressor when it comes to temperature regulation.

Don’t confuse portable refrigerators with electric coolers, as that’s another product category entirely. Electric coolers rely on thermoelectric cooling, which isn’t as efficient because it's impacted by ambient temperatures. As such, they can only cool to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Unlike portable refrigerators, electric coolers don’t have a compressor and don’t have the power to achieve freezing temperatures.

Portable refrigerators typically draw an average of about 45 watts of power, which is less than a standard mini fridge. This won’t blow out any car fuses or drain a car battery unless the unit is kept on for days without the car running. We chose portable refrigerators that have features like eco modes and automatic shutoff so there are precautions in place to prevent it from draining a car or portable battery.

While portable refrigerators offer more storage than coolers because they don’t need ice, their built-in compressor makes them relatively heavy at about 30 pounds or more. Still, some are more portable than others thanks to built-in handles and wheels. They don’t have shoulder straps and aren’t meant to be carried over a far distance. Also, most don't have drain plugs like standard coolers because condensation is minimal and can easily be wiped out with a small towel.

#6221. Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA

As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time.

Endeavour’s new home at the California Science Center in Los Angeles will reopen the weekend of Nov. 13, displayed upright in launch position, ready to inspire the next generation of space explorers.

“Chasing Endeavour’s final ferry flight over Southern California was, without a doubt, a leading highlight of my 37-year career at NASA,” said Lori Losey, lead videographer at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. “I advocated for two chase aircraft to be used in the LA area so we could dedicate one aircraft to photo and one to video. It was this beautiful dance of alternating altitudes and swapping positions between landmarks to maximize both of us capturing the legendary imagery.”

Two photographers and one videographer, all based at NASA Armstrong, had a leading hand in preparing the Endeavour’s flight to Los Angeles, and in deciding where else the aircraft would fly around California on its final journey. Agency pilots planned the route to fly across some of California’s most iconic landmarks and the imagery team strategized about how to best capture the images.

“The most fun thing about this project was seeing the excitement of the people on the ground as we flew over the different landmarks,” said Jim Ross, NASA Armstrong’s lead photographer. “People in the Los Angeles area really came out and supported the Endeavour flyover. We saw so many supporters at Griffith Park and Disneyland.”

Photographer Carla Thomas said seeing the standing-room-only crowd below the California State Capitol in Sacramento filled her with pride. After joining the agency in the wake of the Challenger tragedy, she reflected on the opportunity to document NASA’s return to flight.

Endeavour was escorted by NASA Armstrong’s F/A-18s and an F-15, which carried the photo and video teams in the back seats. Like many flight efforts, this journey took a significant amount of preplanning with the California Science Center, as well as groups like the Federal Aviation Administration, the Los Angeles International Airport, and NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

“The planning was my favorite part of this effort — it was fun and exciting to plan the shots,” Thomas said. “I flew the entire route with the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) in one of their helicopters. We had to make sure this was going to work and find any obstacles. Planning for the Hollywood sign was challenging, because it’s on the side of a hill with power lines and radio antennas, but we worked through these issues in the planning process.”

The space shuttle’s flight path included other California landmarks: Dodger Stadium, the Getty Center, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, the Golden Gate Bridge, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, and the Santa Monica Pier.

Endeavour helped begin assembly of the International Space Station by delivering its first components to orbit and went on to complete 25 missions. The space shuttle will soon be seen, along with some of the images from the final flight, in its permanent home inside the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center in Downtown Los Angeles.

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#6219. The 7 Best Smokeless Fire Pits We Tested (and Yes, They Produced Hardly Any Smoke)

From set-it-and-forget-it backyard centerpieces to grab-and-go options for weekend camping trips, we tried well-regarded options from Solo Stove, Breeo, Blue Sky, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire. They achieve this through two points of combustion: The first happens at the bottom, where airflow feeds burning wood; the second occurs at the top, where the fire’s smoke and gas output are burned off. And while no smokeless fire pit is 100 percent smokeless, if you use best practices (like burning dry wood) they come pretty darn close.

We tested smokeless fire pits in our New York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone. Along with smoke output, we considered size, which affects wood capacity and where the heat actually lands, as well as how easy each pit was to empty of ash and store once done, among other factors. We also used them repeatedly over time to see how their finishes held up, because a brand-new pit can look very different after several fires.

Solo Stove is the brand most people associate with smokeless fire pits (though Breeo was the first game in town). The latest joiner in Solo Stove’s lineup is the Summit, an upgraded take on the ever-popular Bonfire. Its 23-pound weight makes it just as easy to lift and store off-season, and there’s even less setup required. All-in-all, it’s the best smokeless fire pit for most people who want to enjoy a backyard fire pit that can be stored off-season.

Because the Summit is four to five inches shorter than the Bonfire, it does a better job of keeping your feet warm, one of the major gripes our Test Editor Brad Ford had of the earlier model. He says that while it holds less firewood, it undoubtedly produces a higher flame that extends well above the rim.

Another improvement he points out is the Summit’s integrated stand, which he says is sturdier and allows for better airflow than that of the Bonfire’s detached stand. There’s also a deeper ash pan, which is particularly helpful because the Summit burns through wood fast and needs frequent reloading. In terms of price, the 19.5-inch Summit is $100 more than a Bonfire of the same size, an extra cost that’s well worth the investment.

Full Solo Stove Summit Smokeless Fire Pit Review

After trying out the Breeo X Series 24 for several months, test editor Brad Ford loved it. According to Ford, “One of the coolest details of the X Series 24 is its Corten finish. (It is also available in a stainless-steel finish.) Corten is a structural steel alloy you often see used for bridges or power line towers. It’s designed to oxidize, or rust, creating a natural finish that protects the steel rather than continuing to degrade it. This eliminates the frustration I’ve had with some stainless-steel fire pits that discolor after a couple uses.”

Beyond this, Ford also liked, “that Breeo intended for their smokeless fire pits to be used for cooking from the get-go, which means they’ve got accessories for the X 24 that work very well. And most of their cooking accessories are compatible with all their fire pits. Top this all off with the fact that the X 24 is made right in Lancaster PA, USA, unlike most other popular brands.”

The Breeo X 24 weighs more than twice as much as the other models we’ve tested, so it’s not exactly portable—but it is long-lasting.

As the largest pick of the lot, the X Series was easy to load with wood and start a fire. We fit 18- to 20-inch logs into it, laying them across the raised X in the bottom of the pit. This patented design keeps the logs high, allowing air to flow in and feed the fire from the bottom.

Cleanup required scooping ash out, as the unit is too heavy to dump out easily—Breeo sells a shovel designed to ease this process. The brand also offers several accessories for cooking over the fire, which make the X Series as much a grill as it is a fire pit.

This hefty, all-black fire pit is a great-value addition to an outdoor setup. Its wide diameter gives you plenty of room to build a substantial fire, and the shape and airflow make for a good, largely smokeless burn. It takes both wood and pellets right out of the box, no adapter or switch-up required. And the lift-out ash catch has two handles, making it one of the easiest models to empty. (You still have to reach into the drum to lift it out, though, so wear gloves.)

The black coating is practical, too: Unlike stainless steel, it doesn’t show every fire mark. Once in place, it blends nicely with patio furniture, particularly setups with black metal legs. While it does scratch more easily than others we tested, you can touch it up with high-heat spray paint, just like you would a grill.

Some things to bear in mind: At 35 pounds, it’s heavier than many of the models we tested, so you’re unlikely to move it around much once it’s situated. The price doesn’t include a cover, which you’ll definitely want if it’s going to live outside for the season.

Because the ash catch sits inside the main body, with no separate base beneath it, we’d also place this one on a fireproof mat to be extra safe. And this may be petty, but the branding is the most prominent of any pit we tested: you’ll be looking at the words “Blue Sky” on the base every time you sit down.

If you want to bring the campfire with you wherever you go, the Packfire portable fire pit is an ideal choice. It packs down into a backpack, so you can carry it on your shoulders and set it up wherever your adventures take you. In fact, its innovative design won it a spot in our 2026 Home Awards.

The fire pit is composed of three sections: the base, which serves as a stand and ash pan; the body, which, when fully set up, surrounds the base; and the ring, which holds the body in place. Cleanup is easy: Simply lift the ring and body off the base, pour the ashes out, and break everything back down for travel.

It’s worth noting that even though it’s built for travel, the fire pit is still a bit cumbersome to carry around. While our Director of Product Content, Will Egensteiner was testing the Packfire, he said its 27.5 weight was a factor. “As I heaved it onto my back to put it away, I almost tipped over. And I’m not a small guy.”

The substance of this fire pit starts with the box: One of the largest and heaviest we had to maneuver into location for testing (only the Breeo was heavier), moving it really requires two people or a dolly. Some of that initial box weight comes from the generous bag of wood pellets packed inside, but the pit itself, at 45 pounds with nothing in it, is hardly lightweight.

Assembly is a little less impressive. Attaching the legs required a drill, as, while an Allen key and screws were included, some of the holes weren’t perfectly aligned, making the process more fiddly than it should have been. It does, however, come with spare screws.

Once assembled, though, this thing is a very good-looking workhorse. The large bag of wood pellets kept going for about 35 minutes before burning down to embers; produced virtually no smoke; and the heat output was surprisingly high.

Simply by flipping the inside container, you can also fire up 14-inch logs inside. The exterior frame stayed remarkably cool and, given it’s black, didn’t discolor the way the stainless steel ones did. While the inside picked up some black streaks from the flames, they looked more like evidence of a real fire than damage, which we actually liked.

The ash disposal is a true highlight. You don’t have to lift, twist, or tip the pit to empty it: An ash pan slides out from the side, shovel-style, so you can dump the refuse without moving the fire pit at all. It also comes with a perfectly fitted cover, which is particularly useful given how difficult this one would be to haul away when not in use.

This seriously smart, compact fire pit is made for small spaces and taking on the road. It’s lightweight, straightforward to assemble, and comes with six pieces: a pit and ash can that sit on top of one another; two pieces that twist together to form a fire poker (a little tight to sync up, but ultimately quite a useful piece); and a spark screen with a screw-in knob to lift it (also a very nice extra).

Truly, the whole kit is quite remarkable, given the price. The ash catch is also cleverly designed to fit inside the fire pit for storage, so there’s nothing extra to haul around when not in use. The black finish looks sharp and has the added benefit of hiding burn marks better than lighter finishes. (The downside is, it scratches easily.)

The whole thing packs into a carrying bag with a shoulder strap and drawstring closure. It’s also lighter than any other model we tested, making it an excellent choice for beach parties, camping trips, or anywhere you need to carry your fire pit more than a few feet.

There is one important caveat: Because the pit is so compact, you’ll mostly be limited to twigs, which burn quickly. Use wood pellets instead, for a longer, more consistent fire. The carrying bag also feels flimsy, like it could break down quickly with repeat use, but, for the price, that may not matter.

This one looks like a saucer and comes with just three pieces: a main body that locks securely into the ash holder base and a wind guard that twists onto the rim. It’s also one of the roomier pits we tested, with a wider, more-open design that accommodates both more and larger pieces of wood than many others. The manufacturer says it handles logs up to one pound. We’d have preferred a measurement in inches, but went with 16 inches, which it handled better than the Tiki. You can also add a griddle attachment to turn it into a cooker.

This one really does produce a roaring fire that can warm four people comfortably. The wide, funnel-like shape seems to encourage a bigger, more expansive flame; sitting around it felt more like a bonfire than simply burning wood in a container. After 25 minutes, we still had a substantial fire going. Its lower stature kept our feet warm too.

The biggest downside is ash removal. The pan in the base is relatively shallow, and the wide fire pit is awkward to twist and lift off for cleaning. You’ll want long arms—or a second person—to do it comfortably. The stainless-steel finish also turned a light bronze after just one use. A cover costs extra.

Before lighting a single fire, we evaluated the things that can make or break a smokeless fire pit before you ever use them. We assessed the packaging and how well each pit was protected in transit, weighed every model, and evaluated assembly. We read the instructions, noting whether they were clear, complete, and actually useful.

We considered whether it could be disassembled for storage, and what came in the box versus what required an additional purchase. While We had plenty of outdoor space to work with, safety always came first: we set every pit on heavy-duty pavers and kept a fire extinguisher close at hand.

Then we lit them up. We used comparable loads of seasoned firewood to assess how easily each pit started, how much smoke it produced, how evenly it burned, and how much heat it put out. We paid attention to flame height and consistency, too, and whether the fire actually warmed people sitting around it—not just looked good from a distance. We measured logs to see exactly what each pit could accommodate and tested wood pellets where models supported them.

Finally, we evaluated the less glamorous but equally important details: how easy each pit was to tend, how much ash accumulated, how easily that ash could be removed, and what it took to clean and put each model away. And because a fire pit can be beautiful at 7 p.m. and a pain in the ass at 10 p.m., we tested for both.

Whether you want a smokeless fire pit to heat your outdoor space or be more of an ambient seasonal moment is an important consideration. For long nights by the fire with family and friends, you’ll likely want to invest in a larger model that measures 24 inches in diameter. In testing, models that size and up exuded warmth for several feet, and could easily warm four to six people.

They could also handle 14- to 16-inch-long logs. The trade-off: Models this size are a lot heavier and harder to move. If you’re looking for more of a warming accent, narrower fire pits work wonders. You can also maximize some models’ output by adding a heat deflector that sits above the flames and pushes heat out laterally, instead of letting it escape upward.

Ideally, the smokeless fire pit should work right out of the box, with limited-to-no setup, besides setting the pit on a base. It should also break down easily. If you’ll be storing it between fires or seasons, a model that’s easy to disassemble, carry, and put away is key.

The shallower and wider the smokeless fire pit, the easier it is to make a fire from scratch. You simply have more base room to work with to set up your paper, kindling, and wood, and less depth to maneuver to light your fire once ready. No matter your choice, you’ll definitely want a lighter with a long metal wand and a safety catch. None of the models we tested included one.

Burning pellets instead of wood was the closest we got to a truly smokeless fire during our testing. Made of compressed wood waste like sawdust, chips, and shavings, pellets are easy to light, always bone dry, and produce a hotter, more consistent flame than logs. There are trade-offs, though: They lack the classic crackle and pop of a wood-burning fire and that wonderful smell.

Bags of the stuff also typically cost more than a handful of logs at the hardware store, yet burn about the same length of time. But, if you’re allergic to smoke, don’t want your sweaters to smell of it, have wet wood drying out, or want a reliable and even fire every single time, pellets are an excellent way to go. Some fire pits work with them right out of the box; others need an adapter.

Every smokeless pit burns wood. Many smokeless fire pits can also use wood pellets right out of the box. Some, like Solo Stove, need an adapter, so the tiny pellets don’t drop right through the pit’s air holes into the ashcan below. Some portable options may only be wide or deep enough to handle twigs (pellets may be a better option for those).

Pro tip: Wet or green wood will always be slow to burn and emit a lot of smoke; use a moisture meter to suss out whether your logs are dry enough to light up before putting a match to them.

If you plan to use your fire pit regularly, easy ash removal should be a deciding factor. The last thing you want to have to do is pick up and tip a heavy steel drum over a trashcan in order to empty it of ash. Instead, look for a removable ash pan or tray that allows you to lift the ash out cleanly once the pit has fully cooled (usually 12 to 24 hours after a fire has ended). Otherwise, you’ll need a shovel to scoop out the ash.

If you don’t have space to leave your fire pit outside all year, think about who will move it and how often. Even a small pit designed for camping trips can weigh as much as 20 pounds. Fortunately, these options usually come with a carrying bag, so you can sling them over your shoulder. Meanwhile, larger models can top 45 pounds (the 24-inch Breeo weighs just over 60 pounds), which matters when you have to move it under cover or into the garage at the end of the season. Units that come apart make this easier; having a dolly or hand truck on hand helps, too.

Material affects how long your new pit will look the way it does on arrival. While stainless steel looks shiny and modern from the start, heat from the flames will discolor it, and potentially quite quickly, as some testing showed. (You can restore its original shine with a stainless-steel cleaner such as Bar Keepers Friend, but that’s extra work.) Corten-steel usually costs more but forms a protective rust-colored patina that looks attractively weathered over time. Painted or powder-coated steel usually costs less, but can scratch and chip with repeat use.

Whatever finish you choose, keeping your smokeless fire pit empty of ash and covered when it’s not in use will help extend its life. Rainwater sitting in a fire pit full of ash can create a corrosive, alkaline slurry that accelerates rust and can damage the metal. Some models come with a cover as part of their bundle; others charge extra for it. Our reviews note whether a cover is included in every pick.

Smokeless fire pits can be a lot more than a place to warm your hands on chilly nights. In some cases, you can turn them into an outdoor kitchen. Brands like Breeo, Solo Stove, and Cuisinart have grill grates, griddles, pizza ovens, or roasting sticks that let you cook over an open fire. Other add-ons also make a difference, like a cover, if you plan to leave it outside when not in use; a spark screen, particularly if you have toddlers and pets around (though, warning: they can also get hot to the touch); and fire pokers or ashtray lifters, so you don’t get your hands dirty. Definitely check the accessory lineup before you buy your pit; they’re often model-specific. A pair of fire-resistant gloves is always a good investment.

While product photos often depict smokeless fire pits sitting on wood decks or backyards, it’s worth noting that their bases can get hot enough to scorch or discolor lawns, wood decks, composite, and asphalt. Ideally, yours should sit on brick, concrete, stone, or sand. But in the absence of that, a dedicated base (sometimes included, other times sold separately) helps raise the unit off the ground. For an even safer setup, consider adding a fireproof mat underneath. You should also keep a bucket of water or a fire extinguisher nearby and check for local burn bans before lighting. For more on fire pit safety, check out our story.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. #6218. The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory

If there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is showing off Coach's signature cherry bag charm

Bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga shows in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere.

It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing.

Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing says, “think of me on the road,” quite like this.

Bag charms add a pop of color to a neutral bag or suitcase

And there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler.

Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

A little cherry on top, quite literally. Made from glittery resin and metal, this bright red pick brings a playful pop of color to a tote, backpack, or set of keys. It’s a particularly good choice for the friend whose wardrobe could always use one more fun thing.

For the person who prefers their accessories a little more understated—but still appreciates a good detail—this bad boy pairs deep green beads with gold-tone hardware and a lobster clasp, offering their favorite bag a subtle hit of color and texture.

For the New Yorker in your life, here's some Big Apple nostalgia to take on the road. Kate Spade pays homage to its hometown with this mini MetroCard-inspired design—and for those who remember the ol’ swipe of a subway card, it's a fun yet tasteful piece of the city to carry along.

I’m adding this gold boot gem to my cart. For a little Western flair—minus the need to break in a new pair of boots—the iconic brand Tecovas has turned its Loretta boot into a mini accessory crafted from solid brass with an antique finish. It comes with both a key ring and a D-ring, so it can go wherever its owner does—whether that’s a road trip, a dude ranch weekend, or simply the daily commute.

Talk about chic! Sézane’s Juliette keychain has a caramel-color resin exterior with delicate white lace detailing, but the real treat is inside: a pocket mirror that opens with a pivoting mechanism. It’s ideal for a quick lipstick check before stepping off the train or heading out to dinner.

For the friend who has approximately 1,000 photos of their dog on their phone—and would happily add one more to the rotation. This little Jack Russell is embroidered onto supple full-grain leather, with a debossed Lauren Ralph Lauren logo on the back. A rather handsome stand-in for a four-legged travel buddy.

A handbag for your handbag? I’m listening. This mini zippered pouch is styled like a classic carryall, with leather construction and gold-tone hardware, and clips onto a larger bag to keep small essentials close. It’s available in red, cobalt blue, and silver, and can be personalized with a foil-debossed monogram—making it an especially sweet gift for a loved one.

A little luck for the road never hurts! This Madewell design brings together a wishbone, stone, and moon motif in a red-and-gold-toned cluster, and is finished with a dog-clip closure. It’s a playful pick for the friend who loves a meaningful trinket—or could use a little good fortune on their next big adventure.

For the friend who's always planning their next trip, this miniature version of Away’s signature hard-shell carry-on is made from the same durable polycarbonate shell and opens into two little compartments for small essentials like a spare key or folded cash. It clips onto a bag or backpack, and the Coast Blue shade is a nice nod to the real thing.

Meet the mini-me of one of our editors' favorite travel bags. Calpak's best-selling Luka duffel—this compact zip pouch comes in a pearlescent finish and clips onto a larger bag with a carabiner-ready loop. Better yet, it actually earns its keep: There’s room for keys, earbuds, cash, or whatever small essentials you’d rather not fish around for at the bottom of your tote.

A flower that doesn’t need watering—or a vase. Inspired by the marigolds of Diwali, this three-dimensional design is made from layered Italian leather petals and comes in yellow or orange. The leather leaf can also be monogrammed, making it a thoughtful gift with a personal touch. It’s a lovely way to bring a little color to someone’s everyday bag.

#6217. NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman

A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own.

The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy.

Astronomers will use these observations of a large and varied population of gravitational lenses to construct lens models that will help determine how much mass is in the lensing system’s foreground galaxy – and potentially prove or dispel a theory about dark matter. Astronomers study the amount of distortion of the lensed background galaxies to determine the quantity and distribution of mass in the foreground galaxy, including its invisible dark matter.

Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, providing a comprehensive, high-resolution view of individual objects. Roman sees primarily infrared light and some visible, over a much larger field of view to create panoramas of the universe. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and UV prowess for individual objects.

With Hubble's high-resolution imaging and precise models, researchers should also be able to detect small imperfections in these gravitationally lensed galaxy arcs that would indicate the presence of small clumps of dark matter. Researchers could use these previously undetected clumps to confirm the cold dark matter theory, which predicts the existence of many small dark matter clumps of between a million to a billion solar masses. In contrast, the dark matter halo of our Milky Way galaxy is around 1.3 trillion solar masses.

By studying Hubble lens images in detail, researchers intend to build a super-intelligence tool to efficiently search similar arcs in the upcoming Roman images. The Hubble images are expected to both yield their own results on dark matter and pave the way for analysis of Roman’s larger sample of lenses.

The unique lenses in this image display some of the different characteristics researchers will see as they collect a diverse and numerous assortment of lenses to test in their models. Panel A is an example of an arc-counterarc configuration, in which the lensed background galaxy appears as a duplicated pair of arcs. The lensed galaxy is being magnified by a pair of foreground galaxies whose combined mass bends the light of the background galaxy around them.

Panel F is an Einstein Ring, in which the alignment of the background galaxy and approximately spherical mass of the foreground lens are so perfectly situated that the lensed galaxy almost fully encircles the foreground galaxy. Panel I shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, in which the background galaxy is replicated four times, appearing as smeared dots around the foreground galaxy. Panel C also shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, with double knots that are most likely strong star-forming regions in the background galaxy.

Some of the magnified and warped background galaxies appear blue and some appear red. These bluish arcs indicate young stars, while reddish arcs indicate older stars. Roman and Hubble will explore these differences to better understand how galaxies evolved earlier in the universe.

Most of the foreground lensing galaxies are elliptical galaxies, which are older, denser, and more compact. Lensed images of background galaxies only occur when the mass density of the foreground galaxy reaches a critical point.

But not all of these foreground galaxies are ellipticals, and researchers can use these differences to explore the evolutionary paths taken by these galaxies. In panel G, the foreground galaxy appears elongated, which may be true or a trick of perspective, and in panels B and F, the foreground galaxies appear to have spiral arms.

Panel D’s foreground galaxy has a visible dust lane, which is rare in a lensing galaxy and the kind of detail that Hubble’s sharp, visible-light vision excels at revealing. The lensed background galaxy could be an Einstein Ring, with the dust lane “breaking” our view of the ring. Because infrared light is less obscured by dust, future Roman infrared observations could help determine whether the arcs form a more complete Einstein ring.

These strong lenses were first detected with The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak. Hubble subsequently observed them, and Roman will take further observations. Images like these are an example of the kinds of collaborative efforts that routinely take place between NASA’s Great Observatories to build a comprehensive picture of the cosmos. As Roman joins the family of large space observatories that includes Hubble, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the James Webb Space Telescope, a new window opens onto the universe, revealing sights previously hidden while expanding our cosmic knowledge for all of humanity.

Claire AndreoliNASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov

Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.

NASA's Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe.

Hubble and Webb observations complement each other, providing us with a broad view of the universe.
