Flight cancellations are on the rise in 2026. Since Jan. 1, U.S. carriers have canceled roughly 2% of all flights, according to FlightAware, putting this year on pace for the highest cancellation rate since 2022. And delays remain common: About one in four departures nationwide was delayed between Memorial Day and Labor Day, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

While most flights leave on time, delays and cancellations remain a reality of air travel — whether due to bad weather, mechanical issues, scheduling problems or other unforeseen circumstances, including the recent nationwide ground stop.

In case you experience flight delays or cancellations, here are tips on how to decrease your chances of getting stuck and increase your odds of arriving at your destination as quickly as possible. Plus, check out our advice on how to potentially get reimbursed for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation, depending on the reason that caused the delay.

In this era of full flights and easily available information, don’t wait for the airline to tell you there is a problem. You can keep an eye on general flight trends across the country by using FlightAware, which gives you a good overview of how a day in the sky looks.

FlightAware’s “MiseryMap” focuses on delays. In the 24 hours before travel, you can manually check the status of your flight on your airline’s website. If possible, be sure to check the plane's origin. Even if the conditions are clear where you are, there’s a good chance your plane won’t get to you on time if it’s sitting in a snowstorm somewhere else.

It’s also a good idea to sign up for flight notifications from your airline. Here are details on how to opt in to that process with American Airlines and United Airlines.

You can also get flight status updates sent directly from FlightAware. TPG staffers are also fond of the Flighty app, which offers a reliable "Where's My Plane?" feature to track your plane starting 25 hours before your flight.

Be sure to download your airline’s app on your phone, too. Many airlines will show you where your incoming plane is currently. In fact, your airline’s app often has more up-to-date flight departure information than what’s on the departure and arrival boards at the airport.

This can be a tricky one. If your flight is still listed as “on time” in the app, leave for the airport according to the original schedule.

Even if your flight shows as delayed in the app, that status is subject to change. So, in most cases, it’s best to be at the airport ready to go at the originally scheduled time. We’ve certainly heard stories of flights being delayed only to depart sooner than expected, leaving some passengers behind.

Sometimes, you’ll receive confirmation well in advance, letting you know if your flight will be significantly delayed. Say you are at an airport that isn’t a hub for the airline you are flying (meaning there's less chance of spare planes and crew), and the plane that's supposed to operate your flight is nowhere close to arriving at the airport. In that case, it's likely that your posted delay will be a real delay. However, it’s still safer to be at the airport, just in case.

Bad weather can sometimes cause a temporary ground stop at the airport. As soon as the weather improves and the stop lifts, airlines will try to get their flights off the ground ASAP. So, it’s best to be close by should things change on short notice.

Related: 3 things to do if your flight is delayed

It’s important to know your rights as an airline passenger, which have been changed in recent years.

For instance, if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed and you choose not to travel, you’re entitled to a refund, no matter the reason for the disruption. According to current rules from the U.S. Department of Transportation, passengers on domestic flights that are significantly changed, including arriving three or more hours late, and international flights arriving six or more hours late are entitled to automatic refunds if they choose not to travel and don't accept alternative transportation or travel credits. Those refunds must be issued within seven days for credit card purchases and 20 days for cash payments.

However, if you get stranded overnight, you may also be able to recoup costs for extra meals, hotel nights and ground transportation, depending on the reason for the delay. A widespread FAA ground stop, for example, is unlikely to be a covered reason.

You’ll find these and other passenger rights guarantees on flightrights.gov, the DOT’s dashboard.

On that website, you’ll find a rundown of what airlines guarantee in the event of “controllable” delays and cancellations — disruptions within an airline’s control. Keep in mind that these controllable situations typically exclude weather-related problems.

When looking at the dashboard, you’ll quickly see that some airlines promise to do more than others regarding overnight hotel stays, ground transportation, credit vouchers and rebooking on partners. Give that list a look not only when you’re deciding which airline to book with but also in the event of a long, controllable delay or cancellation. This way, you’ll know what the airline has promised to do in those situations. You can file a complaint with the DOT if the airline doesn’t hold up its end of the bargain.

Monitor weather patterns a few days before your flight to see if any major systems are anticipated. It’s vital to check the forecast the night before and on the day of travel to see how any issues could affect your departure and arrival airports.

Again, be sure to opt in to receive updates on your flight’s status. If you know bad weather is coming later in the day, ask for an earlier flight if you can. Alternatively, leaving the night before the weather arrives is a good idea if you want to minimize the risk of delays.

Many airlines will issue travel advisories during (and ahead of) severe weather, such as blizzards, ice storms or even heavy thunderstorms. These advisories allow travelers to make changes even when flying on a restrictive ticket that typically can’t be altered — like some basic economy fares. In some cases, the airline may even proactively change your flight.

If you know bad weather is on the horizon, visit your airline’s website and look for an advisory notice or call the airline to discuss options. If an airline gets ahead of weather issues, you may be able to reschedule your flight by a few days in either direction with no fees. Additionally, you can try asking for a nonstop flight if the weather jeopardizes your connecting flight.

However, if the airline hasn’t issued its own advisory, you might need to pay out of pocket for any fare differences if you really want to be proactive in changing plans.

Standing in a long line at the airport or waiting on hold by phone is usually no longer the most efficient (or most enjoyable) way to rebook when a flight is canceled or delayed.

Most major airlines will allow you to rebook yourself using a mobile app. You may be able to rebook for a new time or even to a new nearby origin or destination city. For that reason, the airline app should probably be your first stop when you learn of a hiccup in your travel plans.

United will even let you standby for up to three flights if something happens to your originally scheduled flight, while maintaining your original seat.

That said, there are times when automated rebooking systems are not your best option. Sometimes, the only automated option is a red-eye flight or a flight several days later that will head to your destination. That’s especially true when many flights are full.

If you can’t locate what you need on the app, find an airline employee who can work the ticketing desk. Check their uniforms and name tags to ensure you get a ticket agent, versus a baggage handler or a similarly outsourced contractor who is less likely to be able to help.

If the U.S. call center has long hold times (which can happen during widespread issues), you can try dialing an international number for faster service. You can often find those numbers on the airline’s website. You might also find success reaching out to an airline on the social platform X or other social media channels when customer service lines are busy.

For example, when the first leg of an American Airlines flight from New York to Arkansas, scheduled just before Christmas, was delayed, TPG Managing Editor Madison Blancaflor missed her connection. She contacted American Airlines on X to help ensure she was rebooked on the earliest possible flight. She still had to endure a long layover in Charlotte, but it was better (and less stressful) than rushing to the customer service desk to try to rebook upon arrival.

Additionally, some airlines offer live online chat or text options that can be quicker than calling.

If there are no reasonable booking options left with your carrier, ask whether there are options available on another airline. If the delay is weather-related and you are on a basic economy ticket or are flying on a low-cost carrier, there might not be other airline options at your fingertips. Still, it’s worth asking — and, if possible, presenting options you have researched yourself.

Related: Don’t wait on hold: Here’s how to reach airline customer service quickly

If you have airline lounge access at a United Club, a Delta Sky Club or something similar, you can head there for help from experienced agents with potentially shorter lines. Use it as a spot to gather your thoughts, charge your phone and make level-headed decisions. The agents there might be able to help you change or track your flight, as there are usually agents with that knowledge and ability in the airline lounges.

In third-party lounges, such as an American Express Centurion Lounge, you won’t be able to get that type of airline-specific assistance, but you’ll probably be in a better spot to wait out the storm than in a crowded terminal.

Related: Best credit cards for airport lounge access

Sometimes, if you really need to get home, you may need to do the work and pay for a new flight yourself.

In some of our prior experiences, the airlines we originally booked with couldn't get us home within 24 hours of our flights being canceled. In cases like these, you may be able to book a nonstop flight with at least one last seat available on another carrier.

Keep in mind, though, that rebooking yourself is typically not covered by any insurance provider or carrier. Still, you should be able to get a refund for your original ticket, which will at least offset some of the pain of a new one. The extra work may be worth it to control your own destiny and avoid being stuck as options narrow.

Your credit card’s built-in trip delay or trip cancellation coverage can help with many unexpected expenses in the face of delays and cancellations, but a brand-new flight home isn’t likely to be one of them. Still, in some cases, it may be the only way home for a while, so you’ll have to weigh the pros and cons.

Fortunately, many airlines now allow you to cancel main cabin tickets and, at the very least, get airline trip credit; you can use this credit to book a future flight — even if you are being proactive to try and avoid possible delays and, ultimately, your originally scheduled flight does not experience a delay. (This does not necessarily apply to basic economy fares or low-cost carriers' flights.)

Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection?

While thinking through what to do in case of a flight delay or cancellation, consider your options at airport hotels; they can fill up during major delays and cancellations. Sometimes, it is best to call it a day, get some rest and try again in the morning.

Airport hotels are generally pretty affordable on points, but cash rates can skyrocket when demand surges. Accommodations are typically covered by trip delay protection in the event of cancellations or very long delays via cards like the (see rates and fees) and .*

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Why my favorite use of Hyatt points is a Category 1 airport hotel

If you know in advance that your flight will be canceled or delayed, heading to the airport early could score you a same-day standby flight that gets you to your destination on time.

For example, one TPG staffer used this strategy to avoid getting stuck overnight when a hiccup with his flight from Austin to New York would have caused him to miss a connection in Dallas. He arrived at the airport a bit early and was placed on the standby list for an earlier flight connecting to a different city.

Getting on the standby list isn’t foolproof, especially if the earlier flight is almost full. This is a case where having elite status can help since you’ll have priority over non-elite travelers. Additionally, some airlines charge non-elite travelers a fee to be added to the standby list for an earlier flight.

Related: The best credit cards to reach elite status

The hard truth is that in the event of airline delays and cancellations caused by weather, the airline itself is not going to help you out with the extra expenses you incur due to the change in plans, since the weather is outside its control. Travel insurance may have your back if you purchased it, but beyond that, the credit card you booked your flight with may also be able to reimburse you for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation — even if it was caused by weather.

Many rewards credit cards confer valuable travel protections when you have a delayed or canceled flight (if you used one of them to book your flight). Below are just a few examples of cards that provide some built-in coverage:

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Best credit cards with travel insurance

To highlight how valuable this can be, a couple of years ago, one TPG staffer's flights home from Colorado during the busy winter holiday season were canceled due to a snowstorm.

She was faced with an unexpected $1,100-per-night hotel stay during peak season in a pricey ski town, based on what was still available at the last minute. Ultimately, her eligible Chase card covered not only the $1,100 unexpected hotel stay but also the unexpected car service and meals during the delay. Within 26 days of the unexpected cancellation and delay, she had a check for $1,401.74 in her hand, thanks to using the right credit card to book the flight.

Unfortunately, some situations are not covered by the built-in trip delay and trip cancellation protections that commonly come with some rewards credit cards, but it never hurts to save receipts and try.

Last but not least, we recommend being decisive when making travel decisions amid delays or cancellations.

The longer you wait to switch flights or book a hotel, the greater the chances you’ll be at the mercy of whatever dwindling options are left as hundreds (or thousands) of other passengers rebook their plans.

Most of the time, your flight will get you where you need to be, close to when you want to be there. Still, flight delays and cancellations are a reality of air travel. If your flight is delayed by an hour or two, there’s not usually much to do other than be patient. However, when facing a long delay or cancellation, it’s good to have a plan to reduce the odds of getting stuck.

Given the common theme of full flights these days, acting quickly, researching options and making a speedy decision will put you ahead of the pack.

#6120. How the Electoral College Dies

Blue-state activists are about to be perfectly positioned to execute an end run around the constitutional system.

In the wake of the 2026 midterms, we are on the cusp of a total transformation of the U.S. election system. After decades of Republican dominance in state legislatures, Democrats now control enough state governments to push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past its 270-vote activation threshold and dismantle the Electoral College from below.

But it seems like the right has barely realized the importance of the fight that’s about to begin.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

As the holidays inch closer, many of you might be wondering what to get for people on your gift list. As a travel expert who’s constantly on the go, I will say some of my favorite things revolve around staying organized and being comfortable — from luggage to passports, I always know where my essentials are, and now that I travel with my kids, it’s even more important.

I’m sharing a few of my favorite things that also make great gift ideas for friends and family.

My favorite, which I’ll always throw in my bag, is my Bose QuietComfort noise-canceling headphones. These are stylish and have great sound quality — the surround sound is awesome. They are my go-to for flights; they are comfortable and connect seamlessly via Bluetooth.

TPG tip: Bose is often on sale during Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale. Make sure you stack any deals with a card that earns rewards on Amazon purchases.

Best for: Getting things done on the go without a laptop

#6118. FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop

Flights were grounded across the U.S. Friday afternoon over suspected air traffic control communications issues.

The FAA issued a highly unusual mass ground stop shortly after 3 p.m.

“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped,” the agency said in an advisory. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.”

In a separate statement, the FAA said a communications issue affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers is to blame. Agency technicians are now investigating the issue.

According to ABC News, this is only the second time since the 9/11 attacks that departures across the country have been stopped. Flights currently in the air are believed to still be in contact with ATC.

National media outlets showed footage of commercial airplanes queued up but not moving at numerous major airports, including Los Angeles, Boston, Reagan National, New York-LaGuardia, Houston Bush, Dallas/Fort Worth, and Raleigh–Durham.

The ground stop will almost certainly cause a cascade of cancellations and delays lasting into the weekend.

The first Cabinet-level official to comment in person on the incident was Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who spoke to reporters outside the White House. Mullin said there is no indication that the outage is a cyberattack, or connected to the recent Microsoft outage.

The situation is close to “unprecedented,” the secretary added, but there is no threat to public safety or reason to panic. Mullin said it is still too early to say when the problem will be resolved.

It was not immediately clear if the outage is connected to ongoing upgrades on ATC systems and infrastructure. The FAA has been moving rapidly to replace outdated equipment, such as old radios and floppy disks, and install more automated technology. The agency is also ripping out old copper wiring and replacing it with fiber optic cables.

#6117. Southwest Airlines Auctioning Off Old Oakland Baggage Tugs For $750

Southwest Airlines is auctioning off several electric baggage tugs previously used at Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) in California, with starting bids as low as $750 per vehicle. The used ground support equipment (GSE), dating back to 2008, has attracted online attention after its unusual auction listing was shared on Reddit. The sale gives aviation enthusiasts and potential buyers a chance to own a piece of airport equipment for far less than a conventional road vehicle.

The vehicles were originally designed to transport luggage and other equipment around airport aprons. While they may look like oversized utility carts, these specialized machines play an important role in airlines' daily operations, connecting aircraft with baggage-handling facilities and terminals. Their retirement from Oakland also highlights how airlines and airports periodically dispose of surplus equipment, creating opportunities for buyers outside the aviation industry.

According to PEOPLE, Southwest is offering several of its former baggage tugs through an online auction hosted on GovDeals. The vehicles were previously operated at Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport and are listed as 2008 Charlatte T137 electric baggage tugs. Each has a starting bid of $750, making them a relatively inexpensive proposition for anyone interested in acquiring unusual industrial machinery.

These vehicles are slightly larger than ordinary golf carts. Each tug measures approximately 10 feet, 5 inches (3.18 meters) long, four feet, four inches (1.32 meters) wide, and four feet (1.22 meters) tall. According to Charlatte America, the manufacturer, the T137 is a self-propelled, battery-powered electric tow tractor designed for airport ramp and industrial material-handling operations. Rather than carrying passengers, it is designed to move equipment and baggage trailers around airport facilities.

Importantly, the $750 figure represents the starting bid, so the final price can be higher. Buyers must also arrange and pay for collection of their successful purchases, and GovDeals requires winning bidders to schedule appointments to remove the equipment themselves. Consequently, prospective buyers must consider transportation, battery condition, maintenance requirements, and replacement-part availability.

Southwest also told Simple Flying that it periodically sells surplus equipment as part of its normal management of equipment and assets.

The auction quickly attracted attention beyond the aviation community after a listing was shared in the Reddit community. The original poster joked about finding someone willing to buy one of the vehicles, prompting a lively discussion about possible alternative uses. Some commenters suggested using the tugs as neighborhood transport, while others imagined turning them into parade floats or even organizing an amateur racing competition.

One particularly practical suggestion was to use an airport tug to move agricultural equipment around a farm. Others pointed out that electric baggage tractors could potentially serve as unconventional utility vehicles for people with large properties. However, their airport-specific design means prospective owners would need to consider charging requirements, mechanical condition, operating limitations, and whether the vehicles could legally be used on public roads.

The Charlatte T137 illustrates the specialized nature of airport ground equipment. Baggage tugs are essential to ramp operations, moving multiple luggage trailers between aircraft and baggage handling areas. Their compact design lets them maneuver around crowded aprons, while electric propulsion offers a cleaner alternative to conventional diesel-powered ground support vehicles. For airlines, maintaining a fleet of reliable tugs is essential to keeping aircraft turnaround operations running smoothly.

This is the story of Unclaimed Baggage, and how a $300 punt became a globe-spanning Alabama-based business.

The Oakland baggage tug sale is not an isolated example of airlines disposing of their surplus ground support equipment. In September 2024, Southwest organized a much larger auction through Starman Bros. Auctions, featuring approximately 119 pieces of equipment located at 31 airports across the US. The inventory included 11 baggage tugs, six pushback tractors, nine ground power units, belt loaders, passenger stairs, heater carts, provisioning trucks, and six forklifts. The inventory also included several ordinary utility vehicles, golf carts, and workshop equipment.

Airports and airlines also periodically dispose of other items they no longer need, including old aircraft seats, cabin furniture, office equipment, and miscellaneous airport property. Even lost-and-found departments can generate unusual auction opportunities. A GovDeals listing illustrates this category, offering a collection of purses and bags classified as unclaimed lost-and-found luggage, sold without their contents and without guarantees about their condition or authenticity.

These sales can attract buyers interested in second-hand equipment, collectors, resellers, and people looking for unusual bargains. As explored by The Guardian, unclaimed luggage auctions have also become a popular curiosity, with buyers sometimes discovering valuable or unexpected belongings inside abandoned suitcases. Whether it is an electric baggage tug, an aircraft cabin seat, or an unclaimed suitcase, the aviation industry occasionally offers the public an unusual opportunity to acquire items that would otherwise remain within airport operations.

#6116. World Of Hyatt Brand Explorer: Free Night Awards For Staying At New Brands

There are several ways to earn World of Hyatt free night award awards. In this post, I’d like to talk about one of the often overlooked ways to earn Hyatt free nights, which is with World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion.

This offers World of Hyatt members the opportunity to earn free night awards for exploring Hyatt’s portfolio. Given the huge brand inflation that Hyatt has seen in recent years, this can potentially offer up to seven free night awards, and counting.

With World of Hyatt’s Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a Category 1-4 free night certificate for every five unique Hyatt brands you stay at. When it comes to earning Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

If you want to see how many Hyatt brands you’ve stayed at, you can do so either through the World of Hyatt website or mobile app. Just go to the “Brand Explorer” section, and there will be a display showing how many unique brands you’ve stayed at (including which ones), and also how many free night certificates you’ve earned.

When it comes to redeeming Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

Of course you’ll maximize value with Brand Explorer by redeeming your free night award at an eligible Hyatt property when the cash rate would be as high as possible. World of Hyatt Category 4 properties can cost as much as 25,000 points per night, and in some situations, could retail for over $300 per night. So if you can find a hotel anywhere in that range, it’s a great way to maximize value.

Hyatt currently has 38 brands, which are as follows:

So as you can see, you’d need to stay at 35 brands to earn seven free night awards. If/when Hyatt adds two more brands, it’ll be possible to earn eight free night awards.

The World of Hyatt Brand Explorer offer is a fun way for the program to engage members and try to get them to try more brands. At least in one case it impacted where I chose to stay, because I do love checking this dashboard every so often, both to see the progress that I’m making, and be reminded of all the brands I’ve stayed at.

Even though I’ve had top tier status with World of Hyatt for over a decade and have now earned lifetime Globalist status, I haven’t even stayed at half of Hyatt’s current brand portfolio. As a matter of fact, I’ve only stayed at 13 of the 38 brands, so that’s just over one-third of properties.

Looking at the Hyatt brands I haven’t stayed at, most of them are all-inclusives, as that’s an area where Hyatt is growing significantly. However, in general this has limited appeal to me, based on the type of travel that I do. I’m sure I’ll knock out a few more brands in the coming years — maybe I’ll get to 15 brands, though I doubt I’ll make it to 20 brands in the foreseeable future.

With World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a free Category 1-4 free night awards for every five Hyatt brands you stay at. This is a way to earn up to seven free nights over time, based on Hyatt’s current portfolio of 38 brands. As Hyatt’s portfolio continues to grow, the opportunities to earn free nights continues to increase.

However, staying at Hyatt’s all-inclusive properties requires some effort, given that they’re not typically places you just drop into for a night.

Given how easy Hyatt makes it to track this, I’m curious — how many Hyatt brands have you stayed at? Which OMAAT reader has the record for the most brands?

#6115. Combat Took on America’s Socialism Fever

The National Review newsletter captured a time in which revolutionary violence tried to join the mainstream.

Young men raise their fists and chant slogans during the “Days of Rage” demonstrations organized by the Weatherman to protest the Chicago Seven trial and “to bring the war home” in Chicago, Ill., in 1969.

Socialism looks in 2026 a lot like bell bottoms: tried on, worn out, and out of fashion.

Decades ago, Germany, Russia, Cambodia, Ethiopia, and points beyond tried socialism to disastrous results. Many American leftists, as judged by the election returns, believe in an American exceptionalism of sorts, too. They think that socialism in the United States will be different. We won’t need a world war, societal collapse, or the obligatory charitable single and accompanying global benefit show to save us from its consequences. Socialism, for its true believers, amounts to salvation and not that from which people living under it require deliverance.

#6114. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

#6113. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

Speaking as someone who is now approaching 17 years of experience traveling with kids, having the right "stuff" matters more than you might think.

Something for the kids to do, something to keep the devices charged, something to hold all the stuff, something to hold the kid and something comfy to wear (with pockets!) throughout the process are just a few of the things that can make family travel a little easier along the way.

So, as we approach the holiday season, here are 11 of my tried-and-true recommendations for gifts, whether you're shopping for yourself or another family on the go.

Best for: Preschool-aged kids who fly frequently

If your family travels a lot and your preschool-aged kid wants a really cool piece of luggage all their own that matches yours, then the Away Kids Carry-On Luggage is a great choice. It's not only fun, but really well made.

It comes in colors such as berry pink and dragonfly blue — and there are even some limited-edition colors and collections, including a current Toy Story line. The handle adjusts to two heights: one for them and one for you when they ... decide to be done. Like the full-size models, it has a TSA-approved lock and a compression system.

Once your kiddos get much past the preschool years, they might be better off with full-sized Away Carry-On bags simply because they hold more. But there are a few good years when these bags are absolutely perfect for little frequent flyers.

TPG tip: Not only does Away sometimes run pretty decent Black Friday sales, but there are periodically Chase Offers that save you $50 or more on certain Away bag orders with cards such as the (see rates and fees).

Best for: Families with multiple devices they need to keep charged on the go

Phones, tablets, headphones — virtually everything requires power on the go these days, so having a good charger for the family is a must. Anker makes some of the best, and one that can be especially handy when you have a family's worth of devices to keep charged is the Anker MagGo Power Bank. It has a kickstand, shows you the battery percentage and time remaining to charge, can charge itself while recharging your devices and can get an iPhone to about 50% power in just 30 minutes.

TPG tip: Anker chargers are sold at many big retailers, so to earn bonus miles or cash back on this (and other) purchases, check CashBackMonitor.com before buying to see which shopping portal is offering the biggest reward for clicking through first.

Best for: Teens and tweens who like taking pictures and having something tangible to show for it beyond photos on their phones

Gen Alpha and Gen Z are into nostalgia — and with that comes photos you can hold in your hand instead of just viewing on your phone. Frankly, I'm here for it.

One of the mini cameras that makes this easy is the Fujifilm Instax Mini 13. It has two self-timer options, a cute design available in five colors and produces instant prints measuring roughly 2 by 3 inches. It's a fun way to give your kids physical memories of their travels instead of having every photo live somewhere in the cloud.

TPG tip: The camera typically does not come with film, so be sure to pick up Instax mini instant film to go with the gift.

Best for: Moms who want to be comfy on the plane but also a tiny bit on trend

Being comfortable when kiddos are involved is often priority number one, whether you're running around at home, navigating an airport or flying halfway around the world.

Enter one of my favorite brands: Vuori, which makes some of the most comfortable clothes I own.

My current favorite is the Vuori Halo Essential Wide Leg Pants in black. They go with almost everything, are cozy for the plane, are made with Vuori's DreamKnit material and have pockets — an absolute must on travel days. They also come in short, regular and long lengths, so you can find the right fit.

TPG tip: If you want even more comfy athleisure in your luggage or under the tree, remember that the comes with a quarterly up to $75 credit for Lululemon (enrollment required). And you can still check to see if Lululemon is on a site such as Rakuten to potentially earn some bonus points or cash back.

Best for: Ages 3 - 10 often love these, but they can really work for virtually any age who likes to hold a 'pen' and draw.

LCD drawing tablets are the definition of punching above their weight (er, price) class when it comes to how much entertainment they provide for how little they cost.

We've had tablets like these draw a crowd at a delayed boarding gate full of children before, especially when Grandma was smart enough to buy a few extras "just in case" since they are so affordable.

They're fun, mess-free, inexpensive and perfect for long flights or car rides. Plus, many are designed to be resistant to some inevitable drops and spills that come with traveling with kids.

TPG tip: Because they are so affordable, it might be worth picking up an extra one.

Best for: Travelers who want to stay organized (honestly, I think everyone who travels can benefit from these)

The list of reasons I recommend packing cubes for family travel is longer than The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King extended edition. But here's the abridged version: You can easily pack by person or by day, stay organized and often fit more into your bags than you could without packing cubes.

And a bonus reason I bet you wouldn't have guessed is that packing cubes can be a good way to help reduce the chances of bringing bed bugs home if you use them in your larger packing and unpacking strategy, as I do. Calpak makes very durable packing cubes that also come in really cute patterns and colors, such as polka dot and dark cherry, alongside classics like black.

TPG tip: Even if you don't pack for the whole trip by day, having a packing cube full of the first night and next full day's worth of clothes so you don't have to dig through all the bags right away is one of my favorite travel hacks.

Best for: Anyone with Apple devices who owns virtually anything they don't want to lose.

At this point, we probably almost all know and love AirTags. But with the second generation now offering improved range, they're even more useful, and honestly, I don't think you can realistically ever have too many.

Put one in each piece of luggage, your kids' backpacks, your sling bag, on your keychain, on your pet's collar, even in your carry-on bags you don't plan to be parted from ... just in case.

TPG tip: You can now share the location of the AirTag you put in your checked luggage with many airlines in case your bag is delayed, helping reunite you with your things faster.

Best for: Travelers who want a sleek, cool, functional bag that looks like it cost a lot more than it did.

I have luggage brands that cost double or more what this Quince bag costs, but it was just as light as those pricier brands I've tried and rolled at least as well with its 360° spinner wheels, had a very smooth and easy-to-use handle and came in a fun dark green color.

TPG tip: The Quince expandable carry-on is the one I was gifted by Quince to try out, and I love the extra space over the traditional carry-on size and it fit in the overhead bin just fine. However, be aware that some airlines (and certain gate agents) can be stricter than others about size limits on expandable luggage and may ask you to unexpand it.

Best for: Families with newborns and young babies

When I look back on our time with little kids, there's one purchase that I'd make a million times over: The Doona.

And I still see parents-in-the-know using it now more than ever for the same reason we loved it once upon a time. The Doona transforms from a car seat into a stroller in seconds, without even having to take your baby out of the seat.

It's fantastic for hopping in and out of cabs, navigating airports and bringing an approved car seat aboard a plane, all without having to lug both a car seat and a stroller.

One caveat: It's rated for babies weighing 4 to 35 pounds and measuring up to 32 inches tall, but in my experience, it isn't uncommon for kids to outgrow it well before their first birthday. For those early months when it works, though, it's fantastic.

TPG tip: You can typically fly with your Doona if you purchase your baby a seat, even though you typically don't have to have them in their own seat until they turn two.

Best for: Parents who love to travel with kids ages 2 to 6 who weigh under 80 pounds

There's an awkward phase of family travel when your kids might be too big for you to want to haul a stroller everywhere with you but still can't be trusted to walk through an airport at a reasonable pace for more than 30 seconds.

And for that phase, having luggage that little kids can 'ride' on can be both handy and fun. One of the brands that offers that is Younglingz with their ride-on suitcases that come in fun themes like unicorns, fire trucks and motorcycles. This way, you are getting your kids and their things through the airport even when the walk starts to get a little longer than you'd like.

TPG tip: If you are purchasing this (or anything) on Amazon, be on the lookout for periodic promotions that can save you $15 to $40 (or sometimes more) by using just a few Amex Membership Rewards points toward the purchase.

#6111. Wild: Stolen Delta Bag Tracked From JFK To DC Bus Stop, Thief Nabbed By Police

It’s not totally uncommon to see bags stolen (or perhaps in some cases accidentally taken) from baggage claim belts at airports. In the past that was basically a lost cause, but thanks to things like AirTags, they can often be tracked.

Here’s an absolutely wild version of such a story, where someone in the miles & points community had their bag stolen, and then someone else tracked it down… hundreds of miles away, and with the help of police!

JT Genter is Editor-in-Chief of AwardWallet and a member of the miles & points community who travels full time. On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, he took to social media to share that his checked bag had been stolen off the Delta baggage claim belt at New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) Terminal 4.

He filed a Delta missing bag claim and police report, and pointed out how “so many irreplaceable memories” were lost in the bag, including all his clothing, medicines, all his toiletries, etc. And he claimed that Delta agents didn’t seem like they gave a you-know-what.

God. So many irreplaceable memories lost in that bag. All of my clothing. Medicines. All my toiletries. Literally so many of my worldly possessions stolen right off Delta's baggage claim belt.And @Delta agents couldn't give less of a shit. Acted like it must happen all the time

That’s obviously incredibly frustrating, though this is a story that had a happy ending less than 24 hours later. JT did have a tracker in his bag, so could keep an eye on the movements of the bag, but he just didn’t say so initially. Apparently the person had pretty quickly taken Amtrak down to DC.

But this is where the story gets truly wild. Jamie Larounis, an Upgraded Points contributor and another member of the miles & points community, coordinated with JT to help. Let me just share Jamie’s version of events:

This might be a story for the history books. Man steals backpack in NY. He takes Amtrak train to DC. I decided to play detective and found the thief with the backpack sitting at a bus station. He boards a bus, but luckily I caught the bus number. I found 2 extremely helpful cops to assist and they found the thief a few blocks away and they nabbed him. They asked me to get in the cop car to ID the thief, and we headed to the police station to retrieve the items.

Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today, but with a little perseverance we got this thief locked up!!! Huzzah!

And by "we", I mean @TheForwardCabin! Jamie used the Tile tracking location to get a visual on our bag and found DC police who were ready to protect and serve.What an incredible end to this story!https://t.co/LvFthwBMqt

When asked what was missing from the bag after it was recovered, JT shared that the guy ditched some clothing, supplies, and custom medical equipment, plus “irreplaceable memories.”

When you consider the volume of bags that are checked, obviously a fair number get lost, stolen, etc. In theory, stealing a bag from a baggage claim belt is really easy — you just take it and leave. However:

Publicly, we of course don’t know anything about this thief. Are we to assume that he wasn’t actually flying, and was just there to steal a bag? And of all the bags he could steal, why did that black backpack catch his eye? And was he planning to travel to DC anyway, and if so, was that the plan all along, or was that just the “escape” plan with the stolen goods?

I recognize that people stealing bags off of baggage claim belts probably aren’t the most sophisticated criminals, but in this day and age, you’d think that checking every pocket of the bag for a tracker would be a best practice, given how common they are.

A traveler had their backpack stolen off of a baggage claim belt at JFK after a Delta flight. Fortunately he had a tracker, which showed that the bag was taken down to DC on Amtrak. After posting about this online, someone else coordinated and played detective, and found someone with the bag at a bus station in DC, and with the help of police, it was recovered.

It’s nice when a story like this has a positive ending, and it’s also a good reminder to put some sort of a tracking device in your bag, for situations where your bag gets lost or stolen.

What do you make of this checked bag recovery mission?

#6110. Delta Air Lines Launches New 9-Hour Nonstop Route: See Map Now

Delta Air Lines began operations on a new seasonal route from Minneapolis St. Paul International Airport (MSP) in Minnesota to Kahului Airport (OGG) on Maui. Having not previously been served, not even by Northwest Airlines before it was merged into Delta, Maui was a key unserved market from MSP, with 66,000 passengers flying each year indirectly.

While a domestic route, the length of these flights, which are blocked at almost nine hours in the westbound direction, means that long-haul comfort is required. Delta provides this with the Airbus A330-300, which it operates with 282 seats in a three-class configuration. This new route is seasonal, running until mid-April, and, towards the end of its tenure, coverage will switch from the A330 to the Boeing 767.

Delta Air Lines operated its first flight from Minneapolis to Maui on Monday. According to a corresponding statement released at the time by the Metropolitan Airports Commission (MAC), the Atlanta-based US 'big three' legacy carrier and SkyTeam founding member plans to serve this route five times a week. However, during peak holiday periods and in the spring break, extra frequencies will be added.

Delta first announced its plans to link Minneapolis with Maui back in February, giving nine months for excitement around the route to build. On this front, Amy Martin, Vice President of Network Planning at Delta, said the route "strengthens connectivity from an important US hub while giving Upper Midwest customers more choice."

Brian Ryks, the CEO of the MAC, spoke about the "demand" between MSP and OGG.

"Demand for Maui is high: it’s MSP’s largest unserved nonstop destination. This route will give more options for travelers seeking warm and sunny vacation options over the winter and early spring seasons."

At close to nine hours, the westbound leg of this route is one of the longest domestic services in Delta Air Lines' network. Numbered as DL726, it is scheduled to depart from Minneapolis at 11:53 AM local time. This makes it a handy option for passengers arriving in Minneapolis on early-morning flights. It is scheduled to arrive in Maui at 4:29 PM local time, about eight hours and 36 minutes later.

Of course, with block time including taxi time at both ends, the actual time spent in the air is closer to the eight-hour mark. Data from Flightradar24 shows that, on November 9, the inaugural flight took eight hours and six minutes, departing at 12:02 PM and landing at 4:08 PM. The return leg is flight DL805 and operates overnight, offering ideal early-morning connectivity upon arrival.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

After a planned 90-minute turnaround on the ground in Maui, this service is scheduled to depart at 5:59 PM local time, arriving back in Minneapolis at 5:34 AM the next day. This gives it a block time of even hours and 35 minutes. The inaugural iteration of this leg on Monday spent seven hours and nine minutes in the air, taking off at 6:13 PM local time and touching down at 5:22 AM.

Delta unveils its biggest Delta One overhaul in years, featuring luxury dining, enhanced comfort and global expansion in 2027.

According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, Delta plans to operate a grand total of 100 rotations on this route with the Airbus A330-300, lasting until late March. However, with the corridor continuing to be served until mid-April, it has thereafter penciled in a further 15 round trips between MSP and Maui with the Boeing 767-300ER. A similar switch is planned for its other MSP-Hawaii route.

This corridor links Minneapolis with Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) in Honolulu. Delta serves this route daily with the A330-300 over the winter, but in mid-April, it will also switch to the 767-300ER. This will correspond to a reduction in frequency to four flights a week, highlighting the fact that demand for Hawaii is strongest in winter.

#6109. The Republican Party Must Be Bigger Than Any One Person

The GOP’s future depends on putting principles first.

President Ronald Reagan gives his acceptance speech at the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas

In 1967, Ronald Reagan offered a reminder about the Republican Party that is as relevant today as it was nearly 60 years ago: “Unity does not require unanimity of thought.” Reagan understood something fundamental about political leadership: A party is not a personality cult. It is a coalition of Americans united by shared principles, even when they disagree about policy specifics.

In the aftermath of the midterm elections, Republicans have serious questions to confront. The results demand reflection and an examination of what we believe and what kind of political institution we intend to be. I believe in the Constitution, limited government, individual liberty, fiscal responsibility, and personal accountability. Those convictions have not changed because of political pressure, nor are they dependent on who occupies the White House.

#6108. Update: FAA Lifts Ground Stop

After a roughly five-hour freeze on virtually all commercial aircraft departures, the FAA has lifted its nationwide emergency ground stop.

The FAA canceled the ground stop around 8:20 p.m., and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed it at a press conference at the White House Friday night. He said it will take some time for flights to restart but emphasized that the air space is safe.

According to Duffy, FAA personnel began to see inconsistencies in air traffic data around 3:30 p.m. Friday, and, out of an abundance of caution, the decision was made to ground flights not already in the air. He said old analog ATC communications switches were overwhelmed and “went down,” causing the inconsistency.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the failure was triggered by an attempted technology update, which caused the system to reboot and crash.

There is no evidence of a cyberattack or terrorism, Mullin emphasized, and passengers were never in any danger.

Duffy said travelers should contact their airline for information about potential cancellations and delays. He said his department is in contact with the major carriers and will work with them to restore normal operations.

A small number of mostly international flights were cleared for takeoff at airports such as New York-JFK, Washington Dulles, Reagan National, and Detroit Friday afternoon during the ground stop, but most remained grounded until the FAA reversed its order.

#6107. Chase Sapphire Reserve Business Bonus: 200K Points Welcome Offer

The Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ is Chase’s premium business card. While the card has a steep annual fee, it also has strong perks, and for many people, will prove to be more than worthwhile.

We’re currently seeing a highest-ever Sapphire Reserve Business bonus, which matches the best bonus we’ve seen on this card. I’d like to recap the details of the offer, including talking about eligibility, and why the card could be worth it. While this is a limited time welcome offer, the end date hasn’t been published.

Link: Learn more about the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business currently has a limited time highest-ever welcome offer of 200,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards after spending $30,000 within the first six months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus on this card is worth $3,400, which is incredible, among the best welcome offers out there. Admittedly the spending requirement is big (you need to average $5,000 per month in spending over six months), but so is the bonus.

For context on the Sapphire Reserve Business bonus history, when the card launched in 2025, we saw the same offer that’s currently available, for 200,000 points. Then in early 2026 we saw an offer for 150,000 points, before the offer for 200,000 points returned. Initially the offer for 200,000 points was supposed to end in September 2026, but it was extended, though we don’t know the official end date.

When it comes to applying for the Chase Sapphire Reserve Business, eligibility is unrelated to that of any other Chase Sapphire or Chase Ink card. That means if you’re eligible for business credit cards, you should be eligible for the welcome offer on this card, making this offer pretty widely available.

Keep in mind the general rules of applying for Chase cards, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (though select business cards don’t count toward that total).

If you’re trying to understand general Chase business card restrictions, the Chase Ink cards probably give you the best sense of what you can expect in terms of eligibility. You don’t need a corporation to apply for the Sapphire Reserve Business, as a sole proprietorship would qualify as well. So even a side gig (like freelancing or having a rental property) would potentially qualify you for the card.

There’s not a specific credit score you need to get approved for the Sapphire Reserve Business, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that goes into deciding on approvals.

The $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve Business is a pretty compelling business card. As is the case with many premium cards, the idea is that the annual fee can be justified based on a combination of the rewards structure, benefits, and airport lounge access, among other things.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business bonus currently offers up to 200,000 Ultimate Rewards points, which is in line with the highest ever publicly available welcome offers that we’ve seen on the card.

#6106. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

The reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

On the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

One way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

We don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

You can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

For avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:

Assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

American even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

In 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a company to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree…

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?
